Variable Length Memory Chains:
characterization of stationary probability measures

Peggy Cénac ††thanks: Université de Bourgogne, Institut de Mathématiques de Bourgogne, IMB UMR 5584 CNRS, 9 rue Alain Savary - BP 47870, 21078 DIJON CEDEX, France.    Brigitte Chauvin ††thanks: Université Paris-Saclay, UVSQ, CNRS UMR 8100, Laboratoire de Mathématiques de Versailles, 78000 Versailles, France    Camille Noûs ††thanks: Cogitamus Laboratory    Frédéric Paccaut and Nicolas Pouyanne22footnotemark: 2 ††thanks: Laboratoire Amiénois de Mathématique Fondamentale et Appliquée, CNRS UMR 7352, Université de Picardie Jules Verne, 33 rue Saint-Leu, 80039 Amiens, France.
Abstract

Variable Length Memory Chains (VLMC), which are generalizations of finite order Markov chains, turn out to be an essential tool to modelize random sequences in many domains, as well as an interesting object in contemporary probability theory. The question of the existence of stationary probability measures leads us to introduce a key combinatorial structure for words produced by a VLMC: the Longest Internal Suffix. This notion allows us to state a necessary and sufficient condition for a general VLMC to admit a unique invariant probability measure.

This condition turns out to get a much simpler form for a subclass of VLMC: the stable VLMC. This natural subclass, unlike the general case, enjoys a renewal property. Namely, a stable VLMC induces a semi-Markov chain on an at most countable state space. Unfortunately, this discrete time renewal process does not contain the whole information of the VLMC, preventing the study of a stable VLMC to be reduced to the study of its induced semi-Markov chain. For a subclass of stable VLMC, the convergence in distribution of a VLMC towards its stationary probability measure is established.

Finally, finite state space semi-Markov chains turn out to be very special stable VLMC, shedding some new light on their limit distributions.

MSC 2010: 60J05, 60C05, 60G10.

Keywords: Variable Length Memory Chains, stationary probability measure, Longest Internal Suffix, stable context trees, Semi-Markov Chains.

1 Introduction

In a Variable Length Memory Chain (VLMC), unlike fixed order Markov chains, the probability to predict the next symbol depends on a possibly unbounded part of the past, the length of which depends on the past itself. These relevant parts of pasts are called contexts. They are stored in a context tree. With each context is associated a probability distribution prescribing the conditional probability of the next symbol, given this context.

In this paper we obtain some necessary and sufficient conditions to ensure existence and uniqueness of a stationary probability measure for a general VLMC.

Pending a complete presentation in Section 2, let us now introduce a few objects, notably the combinatorial notion of alpha-LIS (LIS for Longest Internal Suffix), on which our main result is based. Let 𝒜{\mathscr{A}} be a finite set, called the alphabet. A so-called context tree is a saturated tree 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} on this alphabet, i.e. a tree such that each node has 00 or #​𝒜\#{\mathscr{A}} children. The leaves and the infinite branches of 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} are called contexts. The set of contexts, supposed to be at most countable, is denoted by 𝒞{\mathscr{C}}.

To each context c∈𝒞c\in{\mathscr{C}} is attached a probability distribution qcq_{c} on 𝒜{\mathscr{A}}. Endowed with this probabilistic structure, such a tree is named a probabilised context tree. Let ℛ{\mathscr{R}} be the set of right-infinite words on the alphabet 𝒜{\mathscr{A}}. The related VLMC is defined as the ℛ{\mathscr{R}}-valued Markov chain (Un)n⩾0\left(U_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} whose transitions are given by

∀n⩾0,∀α∈𝒜,𝐏⁡(𝐔𝐧+𝟏=α​𝐔𝐧|𝐔𝐧)=𝐪cont⁡(𝐔𝐧)​(α),\forall n\geqslant 0,\penalty\ \forall\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}},\penalty\ \Proba\left(U_{n+1}=\alpha U_{n}|U_{n}\right)=q_{\pref\left(U_{n}\right)}\left(\alpha\right), (1)

where cont⁡(u)∈𝒞\pref(u)\in{\mathscr{C}} is defined as the only prefix of the right-infinite word uu appearing as a context. See Figure 1 for an example of context tree.

If π\pi is a probability measure on ℛ{\mathscr{R}}, asking π\pi to be stationary for such a Markov chain (Un)n\left(U_{n}\right)_{n} amounts to saying that, for any finite word ww which writes w=α​vw=\alpha v where α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}} and where vv is a non-internal finite word of the context tree,

π⁡(w​ℛ)=qcont⁡(v)​(α)​π​(v​ℛ).\pi\left(w{\mathscr{R}}\right)=q_{\pref(v)}\left(\alpha\right)\pi\left(v{\mathscr{R}}\right). (2)

In this equality, w​ℛw{\mathscr{R}} denotes the set of all right-infinite words that begin by ww. This formula applies again for π⁡(v​ℛ)\pi\left(v{\mathscr{R}}\right), and so on, and so forth, until… it is not possible anymore, which means that the suffix of w{w} is of the form α​s\alpha s where α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}} and ss is an internal word of the context tree. This leads to pointing out the following unique decomposition of any finite word ww:

w=β1​β2​…​βpw​αw​sw,w=\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\dots\beta_{p_{w}}\alpha_{w}s_{w},

Consequently, for any stationary measure π\pi and for any finite non-empty word ww, write w=v​αw​sww=v\alpha_{w}s_{w} where vv is a finite word and αw​sw\alpha_{w}s_{w} is the alpha-LIS of ww so that iterating Formula (2) gives

casc⁡(w)=∏1⩽k⩽pwqcont⁡(βk+1​…​βpw​αw​sw)​(βk).\casc(w)=\prod_{1\leqslant k\leqslant p_{w}}q_{\pref\left(\beta_{k+1}\dots\beta_{p_{w}}\alpha_{w}s_{w}\right)}(\beta_{k}).

Elementary arguments on measures show thus that any stationary probability measure on ℛ{\mathscr{R}} is determined by its value on the cylinders based on alpha-LIS of contexts. Denote by 𝒮{\mathscr{S}} the set of alpha-LIS of finite contexts. This set is at most countable. Using Formulas (2) and (3), as developed in the proof of Theorem 2.18, it turns out that, whenever π\pi is stationary, all the π⁡(α​s​ℛ)\pi\left(\alpha s{\mathscr{R}}\right), for α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}} are related by the linear system

π⁡(α​s​ℛ)=∑β​t∈𝒮π⁡(β​t​ℛ)​Qβ​t,α​s,\pi\left(\alpha s{\mathscr{R}}\right)=\sum_{\beta t\in{\mathscr{S}}}\pi\left(\beta t{\mathscr{R}}\right)Q_{\beta t,\alpha s},

where the square matrix Q=(Qα​s,β​t)(α​s,β​t)∈𝒮2Q=\left(Q_{\alpha s,\beta t}\right)_{(\alpha s,\beta t)\in{\mathscr{S}}^{2}} is defined by

Qα​s,β​t=∑c∈𝒞fc=t⋯c=⋯[αs]casc⁡(β​c).Q_{\alpha s,\beta t}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f}\\[2.0pt] c=t\cdots\\[1.0pt] c=\cdots[\alpha s]\end{subarray}}\casc\left(\beta c\right).

In this formula, 𝒞f{\mathscr{C}}^{f} denotes the set of finite contexts, the notation c=⋯[αs]c=\cdots[\alpha s] means that α​s\alpha s is the alpha-LIS of cc, while c=t⋯c=t\cdots means that tt is a prefix of cc. In otherwords, (π⁡(α​s​ℛ))α​s∈𝒮\left(\pi\left(\alpha s{\mathscr{R}}\right)\right)_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}} is a left-fixed vector of the matrix QQ. The study of the matrix QQ indexed by the alpha-LIS of contexts is a key tool to characterize a stationary measure for the VLMC. Our main result, namely Theorem 2.18, has the following weaker version that can be now stated.

Theorem.

Let (𝒯,q)({\mathscr{T}},q) be a probabilised context tree and UU the associated VLMC. Assume that ∀α∈𝒜\forall\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}}, ∀c∈𝒞\forall c\in{\mathscr{C}}, qc​(α)≠0q_{c}(\alpha)\not=0. Then UU admits a unique stationary probability measure if and only if the three following points are satisfied:

  • (i)

    ∀α​s∈𝒮\forall\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}, the cascade series ∑c∈𝒞f,c=⋯[αs]casc(c)\displaystyle\sum_{c\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f},\penalty\ c=\cdots[\alpha s]}\casc(c) converge. The sum is denoted by κα​s\kappa_{\alpha s}.

  • (ii)

    The matrix QQ admits a unique line of left-fixed vectors.

  • (iii)

    For any left-fixed vector (vα​s)α​s∈𝒮\left(v_{\alpha s}\right)_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}} of QQ, ∑α​s∈𝒮vα​s​κα​s<+∞\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}}v_{\alpha s}\kappa_{\alpha s}<+\infty.

The state space ℛ{\mathscr{R}} of a VLMC is uncountable, placing the question of existence and unicity of its invariant probability measures outside of the well marked out theory of Markov chains on countable state spaces. Theorem 2.18 comes down to searching and studying left-fixed vectors of the at most countable matrix QQ.

When 𝒮{\mathscr{S}} is finite, condition (iii) in the previous theorem is automatically satisfied as soon as (i) holds. Furthermore, in that case, preceding condition (ii) gets a complete answer thanks to finite dimensional linear algebra. In the very particular case of stable context trees (see hereafter for a definition) having a finite set of context alpha-LIS, Theorem 3.24 gives a complete characterization of VLMC’s that admit stationary probability measures, which reduces to the convergence of the cascade series.

Note that the characterization given in the previous theorem is expressed via the cascades and the probability distributions qcq_{c}. Nevertheless, the role of context alpha-LIS suggests that the shape of the context tree matters a lot.

The case of stable trees is particularly interesting, Section 3 is devoted to this case. In particular, when a context tree is stable, the corresponding VLMC ends up owning renewal properties, which is not the case for a non-stable VLMC – see Remark 3.5.

A tree is said stable when it is stable by the shift. In other words, for any letter α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}} and for any finite word ww, if α​w∈𝒯\alpha w\in{\mathscr{T}} then w∈𝒯w\in{\mathscr{T}}. See Section 3.1 for a complete definition. In the stable case, the crux of the matter is that the matrix QQ is always stochastic and can be interpreted as the transition matrix of some Markov chain on the set of context alpha-LIS. Indeed, when a VLMC (Un)(U_{n}) is stable, if one denotes by ZnZ_{n} the alpha-LIS of cont⁡(Un)\pref(U_{n}), it turns out that the process (Zn)(Z_{n}) is an 𝒮{\mathscr{S}}-valued semi-Markov chain. This induced semi-Markov chain brings out some renewal times which are the moments cont⁡(Un)\pref(U_{n}) changes its alpha-LIS. All this is detailed in Section 3.2.2.

It should be noticed that studying a stable VLMC (Un)(U_{n}) is not just about studying the semi-Markov chain (Zn)(Z_{n}) mentioned above. Indeed, the trajectories of (Un)(U_{n}) cannot be recovered from the trajectories of (Zn)(Z_{n}). See Remark 3.13. However, it is the properties of the matrix QQ detailed in Section 3.3 that provide increasingly simple and manipulable necessary and sufficient condition for existence and unicity of a stationary probability measure for (Un)(U_{n}) in Theorem 3.19 and Theorem 3.24. The latter theorem also provides the convergence of the distributions of UnU_{n} to the stationary probability measure.

As a final remark, we add in Section 3.5 another link between semi-Markov chains and VLMC: it is shown that any semi-Markov chain on a finite state space is a VLMC associated with some particular infinite stable probabilised context tree. Consequently, one deduces from Theorem 3.24 a necessary and sufficient condition for a non-null semi-Markov chain to admit a limit distribution. The same condition already appears in Barbu and Limnios (2008) for aperiodic irreducible semi-Markov chains as a sufficient condition.

Throughout the text, without drowning the reader in a multitude of examples of context trees, we chose to present enough cases of context trees that:

- answer natural questions about the different assumptions

- sometimes provide explicit calculations

- illuminate results and proofs.

Let us now indicate a non exhaustive range of domains where Variable Length Memory Chains are commonly used. VLMC are random models for character strings. When they have a finite memory, they have been introduced in Rissanen (1983) to perform data compression. They provide a parsimonious alternative to fixed order Markov chain models, in which the number of parameters to estimate grows exponentially fast with the order; they are also able to capture finer properties of character sequences. When they have infinite memory – this will be our case of study – they provide a tractable way to build models which are not finite order Markov chains. Furthermore they may be considered as a subclass of “chaînes à  liaisons complètes” (Doeblin and Fortet (1937)) or “chains with infinite order” (Harris (1955)).

Variable length memory chains are also a particular case of processes defined by a gg-function (where the gg-function is piecewise constant on a countable set of cylinders). Stationary probability measures for VLMC are gg-measures. The question of uniqueness of gg-measures has been adressed by many authors when the function gg is continuous (in this case, the existence is straightforward), see Johansson and Öberg (2003), Fernández and Maillard (2005). Recently, interest raised also for the question of existence and uniqueness when gg is not continuous, see Gallo (2011), Gallo and Garcia (2013), De Santis and Piccioni (2012) for a perfect simulation point of view and the more ergodic theory flavoured Gallo and Paccaut (2013) and Ferreira et al. (2019).

VLMC are used in bioinformatics, linguistics or coding theory to modelize how random words grow or to classify words. In bioinformatics, both for protein families and DNA sequences, identifying patterns that have a biological meaning is a crucial issue. Using VLMC as a model enables to quantify the influence of a meaning pattern by giving a transition probability on the following letter of the sequence. In this way, these patterns appear as contexts of a context tree (Bejerano and Yona (2001)). An appropriate model requires to consider possibly unbounded lengths. In addition, when the context tree is recognised to be a signature of a family (of proteins say), this gives an efficient statistical method to test whether or not two samples belong to the same family (Busch et al. (2009)).

Therefore, estimating a context tree is an issue of interest and many authors (statisticians or not, applied or not) stress the fact that the height of the context tree should not be supposed to be bounded. This is the case in Galves and Leonardi (2008) where the algorithm CONTEXT is used to estimate an unbounded context tree and also in Garivier and Leonardi (2011). Furthermore, as explained in Csiszár and Talata (2006), the height of the estimated context tree grows with the sample size so that estimating a context tree by assuming a priori that its height is bounded is not realistic.

Classical random walks have independent and identically distributed increments. In the literature, Persistent Random Walks refer to random walks having a Markov chain of finite order as an increment process. For such walks, the dynamics of trajectories has a short memory of given length and the random walk itself is not Markovian any more. Recently, as pointed in Cénac et al. (2013); Cénac et al. (2018); Cénac et al. (2017); Cénac et al. (2019), persistent random walks can be viewed as Random Walks with increments built from VLMC for an infinite context tree.

In biology, persistent random walks are one possible model to address the question of anomalous diffusions in cells (see for instance Fedotov et al. (2015)). Actually, such random walks are non Markovian, the displacements and the jumping times are correlated.

There is a large literature on constructing efficient estimators of context trees, as well for finite or infinite context trees. Our point of view is not a statistical one, and we focus here on the probabilistic properties of infinite memory VLMC as random processes, and more specifically on the main property of interest for such processes: existence and uniqueness of a stationary measure.

In Section 2, the definitions of a general VLMC, LIS and alpha-LIS of finite words are given, leading to the main theorem (Theorem 2.18). Section 3 is devoted to the stable case, providing a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence and unicity of an invariant probability measure for the VLMC. The correspondence with semi-Markov model is detailed. Proofs are postponed in Section 4. Finally, Section 5 is devoted to open problems and conjectures.

2 Definitions, notations and main results in the general case

2.1 Probabilised context trees and VLMC

In the whole paper, 𝒜{\mathscr{A}} denotes a finite set having at least two elements, called the alphabet. Its elements are called letters. All main results in the article hold for an arbitrary 𝒜{\mathscr{A}} but, for readability reasons, the proofs are written taking 𝒜={0,1}{\mathscr{A}}=\left\{0,1\right\} whenever this assumption can be made without loss of generality. Let ℛ{\mathscr{R}} be the set of right-infinite words on the alphabet, written by simple concatenation:

ℛ={αβγ⋯:α,β,γ⋯∈𝒜}.{\mathscr{R}}=\left\{\alpha\beta\gamma\cdots:\penalty\ \alpha,\beta,\gamma\cdots\in{\mathscr{A}}\right\}.

The set of finite words, sometimes denoted by 𝒜∗{\mathscr{A}}^{*} in the literature, will be denoted by 𝒲{\mathscr{W}}:

𝒲=⋃n∈ℕ𝒜n,{\mathscr{W}}=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}{\mathscr{A}}^{n},

the set 𝒜0:={∅}{\mathscr{A}}^{0}:=\left\{\emptyset\right\} being reduced to the empty word11 1 In the whole paper, ℕ={0,1,…}\mathbb{N}=\left\{0,1,\dots\right\} denotes the set of non-negative integers.. When v,w∈𝒲v,w\in{\mathscr{W}} and r∈ℛr\in{\mathscr{R}}, the concatenation of vv and ww (resp. ww and rr) is denoted by v​wvw (resp. w​rwr). Moreover, a finite word ww being given,

w​ℛw{\mathscr{R}}

denotes the cylinder made of right-infinite words having ww as a prefix.

A VLMC is an ℛ{\mathscr{R}}-valued Markov chain, defined by a so-called probabilised context tree. We give hereunder a compact description. One can refer to Cénac et al. (2012) for an extensive definition22 2 In Cénac et al. (2012), and in most of the literature on the subject, VLMC are processes on left-infinite words, growing to the right. This convention forces to make frequently use of reversed words in the discourse. Because of this drawback, we make here the opposite choice..

A context tree is a rooted tree 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} built on the alphabet 𝒜{\mathscr{A}}, which has an at most countable set of infinite branches; an infinite sequence r∈ℛr\in{\mathscr{R}} is an infinite branch of 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} whenever all its finite prefixes belong to 𝒯{\mathscr{T}}. As usual, the nodes of the tree are canonically labelled by words on 𝒜{\mathscr{A}}. In the example of Figure 1, the alphabet is {0,1}\left\{0,1\right\} and the tree has two infinite branches: (01)∞(01)^{\infty} and 1∞1^{\infty}. For a finite word w∈𝒲w\in{\mathscr{W}}, w∞w^{\infty} denotes the right-infinite word www⋯www\cdots. A node of a context tree 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} will be called a context when it is a finite leaf or an infinite branch of 𝒯{\mathscr{T}}. The sets of all contexts, finite leaves and infinite branches are respectively denoted by

𝒞,𝒞f​and​𝒞i.{\mathscr{C}},\penalty\ {\mathscr{C}}^{f}{\rm\penalty\ and\penalty\ }{\mathscr{C}}^{i}.

These sets are at most countable. A finite word w∈𝒲w\in{\mathscr{W}} will be called an internal node when it is strictly internal as a node of 𝒯{\mathscr{T}}; it will be called non-external whenever it is internal or a context. In the same vein a finite word or a right-infinite sequence will be said external when it is strictly external and non-internal when it is external or a context. The set of internal words is denoted by

ℐ.{\mathscr{I}}.
Remark 2.1.

An infinite tree on a finite alphabet being given, the fact that it is a context tree or not is not directly related to the growth of the number f⁡(n)f(n) of leaves at height nn when nn tends to infinity. Indeed, f⁡(n)f(n) may grow slowly whereas the set of infinite branches is not countable. Conversely, f⁡(n)f(n) may grow rapidly while the set of infinite branches is countable. One can refer to the first appendix in Ferreira et al. (2019) for more precise statements.

Definition 2.2 (cont of a non-internal word).

Let 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} be a context tree and ww be a non-internal finite or infinite word. Then, cont⁡(w)\pref(w) denotes the unique prefix of ww which is a context of 𝒯{\mathscr{T}}.

For a more visual representation, hang ww by its head (its left-most letter) and insert it into the tree, the head of ww being placed at the root; the only context through which the word goes out of the tree is its cont – see Figure 1.

A probabilised context tree is a context tree 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} endowed with a family of probability measures q=(qc)c∈𝒞q=\left(q_{c}\right)_{c\in{\mathscr{C}}} on 𝒜{\mathscr{A}} indexed by the (finite and infinite) contexts of 𝒯{\mathscr{T}}. To any probabilised context tree, one can associate a VLMC (Variable Length Memory Chain), which is the ℛ{\mathscr{R}}-valued Markov chain (Un)n⩾0\left(U_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} defined by its transition probabilities given by

∀n⩾0,∀α∈𝒜,𝐏⁡(𝐔𝐧+𝟏=α​𝐔𝐧|𝐔𝐧)=𝐪cont⁡(𝐔𝐧)​(α).\forall n\geqslant 0,\penalty\ \forall\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}},\penalty\ \Proba\left(U_{n+1}=\alpha U_{n}|U_{n}\right)=q_{\pref\left(U_{n}\right)}\left(\alpha\right). (4)

The set ℛ{\mathscr{R}} is endowed with its cylinder σ\sigma-algebra, generated by the cylinders w​ℛw{\mathscr{R}}, w∈𝒲w\in{\mathscr{W}}. In the whole paper, the left-most letter of the sequence Un∈ℛU_{n}\in{\mathscr{R}} is denoted by XnX_{n} so that the random sequences grow by adding successive letters X0X_{0}, X1X_{1}, X2,…X_{2},\dots on the left of U0U_{0}:

∀n⩾0,Un+1=Xn+1​Un.\forall n\geqslant 0,\penalty\ U_{n+1}=X_{n+1}U_{n}.
Remark 2.3.

A context tree is never empty because it contains at least its root. The smallest context tree is thus reduced to its root ∅\emptyset. Once probabilised by a single probability measure q∅q_{\emptyset} on 𝒜{\mathscr{A}}, this tree gives rise to the simplest VLMC which consists in a sequence of i.i.d. q∅q_{\emptyset}-distributed random variables (Xn)n\left(X_{n}\right)_{n}. Besides, the tree {∅}\left\{\emptyset\right\} is the only context tree that does not get any internal node. Since the combinatorial aspect of our study is heavily based on internal nodes of context trees (notion of LIS, see Section 2.2), we make the following small restriction.

– In the whole paper, all context trees are supposed not to be reduced to their root. –

Remark 2.4.

When the context tree has at least one infinite context, the initial letter process (Xn)n⩾0\left(X_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} is generally not a Markov process. When the context tree is finite, (Xn)n⩾0\left(X_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} is a usual 𝒜{\mathscr{A}}-valued Markov chain whose order is the height of the tree, i.e. the length of its longest branch.

This section ends by two definitions that will be used in the sequel: our main results on VLMC hold for non-null ones and the shift appears as a useful technical tool.

Definition 2.5 (non-nullness).

A probabilised context tree (𝒯,q)({\mathscr{T}},q) is non-null whenever qc​(α)≠0q_{c}(\alpha)\neq 0 for every c∈𝒞c\in{\mathscr{C}} and every α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}}. A non-null VLMC is a VLMC defined by a non-null probabilised context tree.

Definition 2.6 (shift mapping).

The shift mapping σ:ℛ→ℛ\sigma:{\mathscr{R}}\to{\mathscr{R}} is defined by σ(αβγδ⋯)=βγδ⋯\sigma\left(\alpha\beta\gamma\delta\cdots\right)=\beta\gamma\delta\cdots. The definition is extended to finite words (with σ⁡(∅)=∅\sigma(\emptyset)=\emptyset).

The kk-th iteration of σ\sigma is denoted by σk\sigma^{k} (and σ0\sigma^{0} denotes the identity map on ℛ{\mathscr{R}} or 𝒲{\mathscr{W}}).

2.2 LIS and alpha-LIS, cascades and cascade series

As pointed out in the introduction, the study of invariant probability measures naturally leads to the following notion of Longest Internal Suffix. If w∈𝒲w\in{\mathscr{W}} is a non-empty finite word, ww can be uniquely written as

w=β1​β2​…​βpw​αw​sw,w=\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\dots\beta_{p_{w}}\alpha_{w}s_{w},

where

∙\bullet pw⩾0p_{w}\geqslant 0 and βi∈𝒜\beta_{i}\in{\mathscr{A}}, for all i∈{1,…,pw}i\in\{1,\dots,p_{w}\},

∙\bullet αw∈𝒜\alpha_{w}\in{\mathscr{A}},

∙\bullet sws_{w} is the longest internal strict suffix of ww.

Note that sws_{w} may be the empty word. When pw=0p_{w}=0, there are no β\beta’s and w=αw​sww=\alpha_{w}s_{w}.

Definition 2.7 (LIS and alpha-LIS).

Let 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} be a context tree and ww a finite non-empty word on 𝒜{\mathscr{A}}. With the notations above, the Longest Internal Suffix sws_{w} is abbreviated as the LIS of ww; the non-internal suffix αw​sw\alpha_{w}s_{w} is called the alpha-LIS of ww.

To compute the LIS of a non-empty finite word w=β1​β2​…​βnw=\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\dots\beta_{n}, check whether β2​β3​…​βn\beta_{2}\beta_{3}\dots\beta_{n} is internal or not. If it is internal, that is the LIS of ww. If not, check whether β3​β4​…​βn\beta_{3}\beta_{4}\dots\beta_{n} is internal or not, etc. The first time you get an internal suffix (this happens inevitably because ∅\emptyset is always an internal word, the context tree being not reduced to its root, see Remark 2.3), this suffix is the LIS of ww.

Any word has an alpha-LIS, but the objects of main interest are the alpha-LIS of contexts. The set of alpha-LIS of finite contexts of 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} will be denoted by 𝒮⁡(𝒯){\mathscr{S}}({\mathscr{T}}), or more shortly by 𝒮{\mathscr{S}}:

𝒮={αc​sc,c∈𝒞f};{\mathscr{S}}=\left\{\alpha_{c}s_{c},\penalty\ c\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f}\right\};

this is an at most countable set (like 𝒞{\mathscr{C}}). For any u,v,w∈𝒲u,v,w\in{\mathscr{W}}, the notations

v=u⋯andw=⋯[u]v=u\cdots{\rm\penalty\ \penalty\ and\penalty\ }w=\cdots[u] (5)

stand respectively for “uu is a prefix of vv” and “uu is the alpha-LIS of ww”.

Example 2.8 (computation of a LIS).

In this example, the alphabet is 𝒜={0,1}{\mathscr{A}}=\left\{0,1\right\} and the context tree is defined by its finite contexts which are the following ones: (01)p​00(01)^{p}00, (01)r​1(01)^{r}1, 01r​001^{r}0, 1q​001^{q}00, 1q​011^{q}01, p⩾0p\geqslant 0, q⩾1q\geqslant 1, r⩾2r\geqslant 2.

Take for example the context 010100010100, colored red in the context tree. Remove successively letters from the left until you get an internal word: 1010010100 is external, 01000100 is noninternal, 100100 is noninternal, 0000 is noninternal. In this sequence, the suffix 00 is the first internal one: this is the LIS of 010100010100. The last removed letter is α=0\alpha=0 so that the alpha-LIS of 010100010100 is 0000.

In the following array, the left-hand column consists in the list of alpha-LIS of all the finite contexts of the tree. For every α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}, the list of all finite contexts having α​s\alpha s as an alpha-LIS is given in the right-hand column.

Remark 2.9.

The finiteness of the set 𝒞i{\mathscr{C}}^{i} of infinite branches on one side, and that of the set 𝒮{\mathscr{S}} of context alpha-LIS on the other side are not related. In Example 3.26, one finds a context tree for which 𝒮{\mathscr{S}} is finite while 𝒞i{\mathscr{C}}^{i} is infinite. In the tree of Example 2.8, 𝒮{\mathscr{S}} is infinite while 𝒞i{\mathscr{C}}^{i} is finite. The left-comb of left-combs has infinite 𝒞i{\mathscr{C}}^{i} and 𝒮{\mathscr{S}} (see Remark 3.16). Finally, the double bamboo (see page 3.1) has finite 𝒞i{\mathscr{C}}^{i} and 𝒮{\mathscr{S}}.

Definition 2.10 (cascade).

Let (𝒯,q)\left({\mathscr{T}},q\right) be a probabilised context tree. If w∈𝒲w\in{\mathscr{W}} writes w=β1​β2​…​βp​α​sw=\beta_{1}\beta_{2}\dots\beta_{p}\alpha s where p⩾0p\geqslant 0 and where α​s\alpha s is the alpha-LIS of ww, the cascade of ww is defined as

casc⁡(w)=∏1⩽k⩽pqcont⁡σk​(w)​(βk),\casc(w)=\prod_{1\leqslant k\leqslant p}q_{\pref\sigma^{k}(w)}\left(\beta_{k}\right),

where an empty product equals 11, which occurs if and only if ww is equal to its own alpha-LIS. In the above formula, σ\sigma denotes the shift mapping, see Definition 2.6. The cascade of ∅\emptyset is defined as being 11.

Note that casc⁡(α​s)=1\casc(\alpha s)=1 for any α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}. In Example 2.8, casc⁡(010100)=q101​(0)​q0100​(1)​q100​(0)​q00​(1)\casc(010100)=q_{101}(0)q_{0100}(1)q_{100}(0)q_{00}(1).

Remark 2.11.

Assume that 𝒜={0,1}{\mathscr{A}}=\left\{0,1\right\}. For any w∈𝒲w\in{\mathscr{W}}, casc⁡(w)=casc⁡(0​w)+casc⁡(1​w)\casc(w)=\casc(0w)+\casc(1w) if and only if ww is non-internal; indeed, if ww is internal, the sum equals 22 whereas casc⁡(w)⩽1\casc(w)\leqslant 1. This equivalence generalizes straightforwardly to an arbitrary alphabet.

Definition 2.12 (cascade series).

For every α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}, the cascade series of α​s\alpha s (related to (𝒯,q)({\mathscr{T}},q)) is the at most countable family of cascades of the finite contexts having α​s\alpha s as their alpha-LIS. In other words, with notations (5), it is the family

(casc(c))c∈𝒞f,c=⋯[αs].\left(\casc(c)\right)_{c\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f},\penalty\ c=\cdots[\alpha s]}.

Since the cascades are positive numbers, the summability of a family of cascades of a probabilised context tree is equivalent to the convergence of the series associated to any total order on the set of contexts indexing the family. The assertion

∀α​s∈𝒮,∑c∈𝒞fc=⋯[αs]casc⁡(c)<+∞\forall\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}},\penalty\ \sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{c\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f}}\\[2.0pt] {c=\cdots[\alpha s]}\end{subarray}}\casc(c)<+\infty (6)

will be called convergence of the cascade series. For every α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}} and k⩾1k\geqslant 1, denote

κα​s​(k)=∑c∈𝒞f,c=⋯[αs]|c|=|α​s|+k−1casc⁡(c).\kappa_{\alpha s}(k)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{c\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f}},\penalty\ c=\cdots[\alpha s]\\[2.0pt] |c|=|\alpha s|+k-1\end{subarray}}\casc(c). (7)

When the cascade series converge, κα​s\kappa_{\alpha s} denotes the sum of the cascade series relative to α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}:

κα​s=∑c∈𝒞fc=⋯[αs]casc⁡(c)=∑k⩾1κα​s​(k).\kappa_{\alpha s}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{c\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f}}\\[2.0pt] {c=\cdots[\alpha s]}\end{subarray}}\casc(c)=\sum_{k\geqslant 1}\kappa_{\alpha s}(k). (8)

In the following sections, the convergence of cascade series turns out to be an important part of the characterization of stationary probability measures. This is made precise by Theorem 2.18 and Theorem 3.19. In some particular cases, the convergence of cascade series just becomes a necessary and sufficient condition for existence and unicity of an invariant probability measure (see Theorem 3.24).

2.3 Alpha-LIS matrix QQ and left-fixed vectors

For any (α​s,β​t)∈𝒮2(\alpha s,\beta t)\in{\mathscr{S}}^{2}, with notations (5), define

Qα​s,β​t=∑c∈𝒞fc=t⋯c=⋯[αs]casc⁡(β​c)∈[0,+∞].Q_{\alpha s,\beta t}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f}\\[2.0pt] c=t\cdots\\[2.0pt] c=\cdots[\alpha s]\end{subarray}}\casc\left(\beta c\right)\in[0,+\infty]. (9)

As the set 𝒮{\mathscr{S}} is at most countable, the family Q=(Qα​s,β​t)(α​s,β​t)∈𝒮2Q=\left(Q_{\alpha s,\beta t}\right)_{(\alpha s,\beta t)\in{\mathscr{S}}^{2}} will be considered a matrix, finite or countable, for an arbitrary order on 𝒮{\mathscr{S}}. The convergence of the cascade series of (𝒯,q)({\mathscr{T}},q) is sufficient to ensure the finiteness of QQ’s entries.

The matrix QQ plays a central role in the statement of Theorem 2.18, which is the main result of the paper.

Definition 2.13 (left-fixed vector of a matrix).

Let A=(aℓ,c)(ℓ,c)∈ℰ2A=\left(a_{\ell,c}\right)_{(\ell,c)\in{\mathscr{E}}^{2}} be a matrix with real entries, indexed by a totally ordered set ℰ{\mathscr{E}} supposed to be finite or denumerable. A left-fixed vector of AA is a row-vector X=(xk)k∈ℰ∈ℝℰX=(x_{k})_{k\in{\mathscr{E}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{{\mathscr{E}}}, indexed by ℰ{\mathscr{E}}, such that X​A=XXA=X. In particular, this implies that the usual matrix product X​AXA is well defined, which means that for any c∈ℰc\in{\mathscr{E}}, the series ∑ℓxℓ​aℓ,c\sum_{\ell}x_{\ell}a_{\ell,c} is convergent. Note that, whenever XX and AA are infinite dimensional and have nonnegative entries, this summability does not depend on the chosen order on the index set ℰ{\mathscr{E}}.

2.4 Stationary measures for a VLMC

Definitions and notations of the previous sections allow us to state results on stationary measures for a VLMC. In this section no assumption is made on the shape of the context tree. After two key lemmas, we state the main Theorem 2.18 that establishes precise connections between stationary probability measures of the VLMC and left-fixed vectors of the matrix QQ defined in Section 2.3. Theorem 2.18 is valid for any context tree. Section 3 shows what happens to this result when assumptions (stability, mainly) are made on the shape of the tree. In particular, Remark 3.25 shows how Theorem 2.18 (or Theorem 3.24) applies in the case of finite trees.

Definition 2.14 (stationary probability measure for a VLMC).

Let U=(Un)n⩾0U=\left(U_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} be a VLMC. A probability measure π\pi on ℛ{\mathscr{R}} is said UU-stationary (or also UU-invariant) whenever π\pi is the distribution of every UnU_{n} as soon as it is the distribution of U0U_{0}.

Assume that π\pi is a probability measure on ℛ{\mathscr{R}}, invariant for a VLMC defined on a given context tree. As already mentioned in the introduction, π⁡(w​ℛ)=qcont⁡(v)​(α)​π​(v​ℛ)\pi\left(w{\mathscr{R}}\right)=q_{\pref(v)}\left(\alpha\right)\pi\left(v{\mathscr{R}}\right) for any letter α\alpha and any non-internal finite word w=α​vw=\alpha v. The cascade of ww is the product that arises after the largest number of possible iterations of that formula, so that π⁡(w​ℛ)=casc⁡(w)​π​(αw​sw​ℛ)\pi\left(w{\mathscr{R}}\right)=\casc(w)\pi\left(\alpha_{w}s_{w}{\mathscr{R}}\right). These formulae are the subject of the simple but very useful Lemma 2.15, named Cascade Formulae. Equality (12) can be seen as a founding formula that leads to Theorem 2.18.

Lemma 2.15.

(Cascade formulae)

Let (𝒯,q)({\mathscr{T}},q) be a probabilised context tree and π\pi be a stationary probability measure for the corresponding VLMC.

(i) For every non-internal finite word ww and for every α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}},

π⁡(α​w​ℛ)=qcont⁡(w)​(α)​π​(w​ℛ).\pi\left(\alpha w{\mathscr{R}}\right)=q_{\pref(w)}(\alpha)\pi\left(w{\mathscr{R}}\right). (10)

(ii) For every right-infinite word r∈ℛr\in{\mathscr{R}} and for every α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}},

π⁡(α​r)=qcont⁡(r)​(α)​π​(r).\pi\left(\alpha r\right)=q_{\pref(r)}(\alpha)\pi\left(r\right). (11)

(iii) For every finite non empty word ww, if one denotes by αw​sw\alpha_{w}s_{w} the alpha-LIS of ww, then

π⁡(w​ℛ)=casc⁡(w)​π​(αw​sw​ℛ).\pi\left(w{\mathscr{R}}\right)=\casc(w)\pi\left(\alpha_{w}s_{w}{\mathscr{R}}\right). (12)

A proof of Lemma 2.15 can be found at the beginning of Section 4 on page 4.1.

The following lemma ensures that a stationary probability measure weights finite words and only finite words.

Lemma 2.16.

Let π\pi be a stationary probability measure of a non-null VLMC. Then

(i) ∀w∈𝒲\forall w\in{\mathscr{W}}, π⁡(w​ℛ)≠0\pi\left(w{\mathscr{R}}\right)\neq 0;

(ii) ∀r∈ℛ\forall r\in{\mathscr{R}}, π⁡(r)=0\pi(r)=0.

For a proof of this lemma, see Section 4, page 4.1.

Remark 2.17.

Thanks to Lemma 2.16(ii), when π\pi is a stationary probability measure, both members of Equality (11) vanish. In fact, all formulae in Lemma 2.15 remain true when π\pi is a σ\sigma-finite invariant measure. In this case, Formula (11) may be an equality between two non-zero real numbers. See Remark 2.21 and Section 6 for further comments on σ\sigma-finite invariant measures.

Everything is now in place to state the main theorem. Denote by ℳ1​(ℛ){\mathscr{M}}_{1}\left({\mathscr{R}}\right) the set of probability measures on ℛ{\mathscr{R}}. For a given context tree 𝒯{\mathscr{T}}, define the mapping ff as follows:

f:ℳ1​(ℛ)⟶[0,1]𝒮π⟼(π⁡(α​s​ℛ))α​s∈𝒮.\begin{array}[]{cccc}f:&{\mathscr{M}}_{1}\left({\mathscr{R}}\right)&\longrightarrow&[0,1]^{{\mathscr{S}}}\\[3.0pt] &\pi&\longmapsto&\Big(\pi\left(\alpha s{\mathscr{R}}\right)\Big)_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}}.\end{array} (13)
Theorem 2.18.

Let (𝒯,q)({\mathscr{T}},q) be a non-null probabilised context tree and UU the associated VLMC.

(i) Assume that there exists a finite UU-stationary probability measure π\pi on ℛ{\mathscr{R}}. Then the cascade series (6) converge. Furthermore, using notation (8),

∑α​s∈𝒮π⁡(α​s​ℛ)​κα​s=1.\sum_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}}\pi\left(\alpha s{\mathscr{R}}\right)\kappa_{\alpha s}=1. (14)

(ii) Assume that the cascade series (6) converge. Then, ff induces a bijection between the set of UU-stationary probability measures on ℛ{\mathscr{R}} and the set of left-fixed vectors (vα​s)α​s∈𝒮\left(v_{\alpha s}\right)_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}} of QQ that have non-negative entries and which satisfy

∑α​s∈𝒮vα​s​κα​s=1.\sum_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}}v_{\alpha s}\kappa_{\alpha s}=1. (15)

The proof of Theorem 2.18 is given in Section 4, page 4.1.

This theorem naturally calls for several questions and remarks: for instance, does everything boil down to QQ? Can the theorem be extended to σ\sigma-finite invariant measures? Can Theorem 2.18 be improved for particular context trees? For finite ones? What role does the non-nullness assumption play?

Remark 2.19.

One could be tempted to see f⁡(π)f(\pi) as an invariant measure for some Markov chain associated with the matrix QQ, reducing the study of invariant probability measures of a VLMC to the study of stationary probability measures of the Markov chain associated with QQ. This is generally not true.

First, even when it is finite-dimensional, QQ is generally not stochastic, excluding any hope of interpreting it as the transition matrix of some Markov chain. Take for instance the small context tree on the alphabet 𝒜={0,1}{\mathscr{A}}=\left\{0,1\right\} pictured hereunder. It gets three context alpha-LIS we order the following way: 0000, 1010 and 11. The matrix QQ writes straightforwardly as follows. For instance, its first line’s sum equals 1+q00​(1)1+q_{00}(1).

Second, even when QQ is row-stochastic (which is the case when the context tree is stable, see Proposition 3.15), its probabilistic interpretation is not that simple. In the stable case, QQ can be seen as the transition matrix of the underlying Markov chain of some semi-Markov chain, namely the process of the context alpha-LIS of the VLMC. Section 3.2 is devoted to this fact.

Finally, in general, even in the case of stable VLMC, one cannot reconstruct the VLMC from the process of its alpha-LIS: both processes are not equivalent, the VLMC being strictly richer than the process of its alpha-LIS. See Remark 3.13 for an example and further comments.

Remark 2.20.

Non-nullness appears as some irreducibility assumption on the Markov process on right-infinite words. One can find in Cénac et al. (2012) simple examples of not non-null VLMC’s defined on infinite context trees that admit infinitely-many invariant probability measures.

Remark 2.21.

One may wonder whether a non-null VLMC can admit invariant σ\sigma-finite measures that have an infinite total mass. The answer is clearly affirmative as can be seen on the left comb, which is the context tree shaped as follows, the alphabet being 𝒜={0,1}{\mathscr{A}}=\left\{0,1\right\}: . Once this tree has been probabilised by the non-null family (q0n​1)n⩾0\left(q_{0^{n}1}\right)_{n\geqslant 0}, define cnc_{n} as being

cn:=casc⁡(0n​1)=∏k=0nq0k​1​(0).c_{n}:=\casc\left(0^{n}1\right)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}q_{0^{k}1}(0).

Then, as soon as cnc_{n} tends to 00 when nn tends to infinity whereas the series ∑cn\sum c_{n} diverges, the corresponding VLMC gets an invariant σ\sigma-finite measure with infinite total mass. This can be straightforwardly checked – however, computation details can be found in Cénac et al. (2012).

Moreover, the same argument as in the proof of Lemma 2.16(ii) shows that a UU-invariant σ\sigma-finite measure always vanishes on rational right-infinite words, i.e. on eventually periodic words. One may thus wonder whether a non-null VLMC can admit invariant σ\sigma-finite measures that have an infinite total mass and take a positive value on some irrational infinite word. The answer is also affirmative. An example is developed in the appendix, based on a context tree which has irrational contexts and whose QQ matrix is (necessarily) transient.

3 The stable case

In this section, a restriction on the shape of the tree is put, called stability, defined in Section 3.1. As already said in the introduction, although being very particular, the set of stable trees appears as a very rich class, notably through its links with semi-Markov chains. These links, detailed in Section 3.2.2 (stochasticity and irreducibility of QQ, construction of the induced semi-Markov chain denoted by (Zn)n⩾0\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0}), exhibit renewal properties of the VLMC.

The extra structure brought by the stability enables to simplify the statement of Theorem 2.18, turning it into a necessary and sufficient condition for existence and unicity of a stationary probability measure, for countable 𝒮{\mathscr{S}} (Theorem 3.19) and finite 𝒮{\mathscr{S}} (Theorem 3.24, where the convergence of the law of (Un)\left(U_{n}\right) towards the invariant measure is also obtained).

It must be once again emphasized that the trajectories of the VLMC (Un)\left(U_{n}\right) cannot be recovered from the trajectories of the underlying semi-Markov chain (Zn)\left(Z_{n}\right) (See Remark 3.13). Our results on stable VLMC cannot straightforwardly be deduced from those existing in the semi-Markov literature.

3.1 Definitions

Proposition 3.1.

Let 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} be a context tree. The following conditions are equivalent.

  1. (i)

    ∀α∈𝒜\forall\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}}, ∀w∈𝒲\forall w\in{\mathscr{W}}, α​w∈𝒯⟹w∈𝒯\alpha w\in{\mathscr{T}}\Longrightarrow w\in{\mathscr{T}}. In other words, σ⁡(𝒯)⊆𝒯\sigma({\mathscr{T}})\subseteq{\mathscr{T}}.

  2. (ii)

    If cc is a finite context and α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}}, then α​c\alpha c is non-internal.

  3. (iii)

    𝒯⊆𝒜​𝒯{\mathscr{T}}\subseteq{\mathscr{A}}{\mathscr{T}}, where 𝒜​𝒯={α​w,α∈𝒜,w∈𝒯}{\mathscr{A}}{\mathscr{T}}=\{\alpha w,\penalty\ \alpha\in{\mathscr{A}},\penalty\ w\in{\mathscr{T}}\}.

  4. (iv)

    For any VLMC (Un)n\left(U_{n}\right)_{n} associated with 𝒯{\mathscr{T}}, the process (Cn)n∈ℕ:=(cont⁡(Un))n∈ℕ\left(C_{n}\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}:=\left(\pref\left(U_{n}\right)\right)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} is a Markov chain with state space 𝒞{\mathscr{C}}.

A proof of this Proposition 3.1 can be found in Section 4.2, page 4.2.

Definition 3.2 (shift-stable tree, stable VLMC).

A context tree is shift-stable33 3 This property of trees is also called 00-subperiodic by some authors, like Lyons (1990); Lyons and Peres (2017) or shift-invariant by Furstenberg (1967)., shortened in the sequel as stable when one of the four equivalent conditions of Proposition 3.1 is satisfied. A VLMC is also called stable when it is defined by a probabilised stable context tree.

The following two lemmas, which do not hold for general trees, will be used to get an accurate description of the structure of the context alpha-LIS process, as developed in Section 3.2.2.

Lemma 3.3.

Let 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} be a stable context tree.

(i) Any context alpha-LIS is a context. In otherwords, 𝒮⊆𝒞{\mathscr{S}}\subseteq{\mathscr{C}}.

(ii) Assume that cc is a finite context having α​s\alpha s as an alpha-LIS. Then all σk​(c)\sigma^{k}(c), 0⩽k⩽|c|−|α​s|0\leqslant k\leqslant|c|-|\alpha s| are also contexts having α​s\alpha s as an alpha-LIS.

Proof.

Let α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}} and let c=⋯[αs]∈𝒞fc=\cdots[\alpha s]\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f} (notation (5)). Since 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} is stable, for any k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, the node σk​(c)\sigma^{k}(c) is either internal or a context. By maximality of ss, this implies that the σk​(c)\sigma^{k}(c), for 0⩽k⩽|c|−|α​s|0\leqslant k\leqslant|c|-|\alpha s|, have α​s\alpha s as a suffix and are noninternal, thus contexts. This proves (ii), thus (i). ∎

Lemma 3.4.

Let 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} be a stable context tree and c∈𝒞c\in{\mathscr{C}}. Let 𝒜c:={α∈𝒜,α​c∉𝒞}{\mathscr{A}}_{c}:=\{\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}},\alpha c\notin\penalty\ {\mathscr{C}}\}. Then,

  1. 1.

    if 𝒜c=∅{\mathscr{A}}_{c}=\emptyset, then cc does not admit any context LIS as a prefix;

  2. 2.

    for every α∈𝒜c\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}}_{c}, there exists a unique context LIS tαt_{\alpha} such that

    (i) c=tα⋯c=t_{\alpha}\cdots

    (ii) α​tα∈𝒞\alpha t_{\alpha}\in{\mathscr{C}}.

    Furthermore, for every β∉𝒜c\beta\notin{\mathscr{A}}_{c}, β​tα∉𝒞\beta t_{\alpha}\notin{\mathscr{C}}.

The proof of this lemma is given in Section 4, page 4.2.

Note in passing the following formula, proven during the proof of Proposition 3.1 and valid in the case of stable context trees: if s∈ℛs\in{\mathscr{R}} is a right-infinite word and if α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}} is any letter, then

cont⁡(α​s)=cont⁡(α​cont⁡(s)).\pref(\alpha s)=\pref\left(\alpha\pref(s)\right).

This formula is the foundation for the renewal properties of stable VLMC’s, as described hereunder. For any n⩾0n\geqslant 0 and for any letter β\beta, because of this formula, cont⁡(β​Un)\pref\left(\beta U_{n}\right) depends on UnU_{n} only through its cont. More precisely, if CnC_{n} denotes cont⁡(Un)\pref\left(U_{n}\right), then cont⁡(β​Un)=cont⁡(β​Cn)\pref\left(\beta U_{n}\right)=\pref\left(\beta C_{n}\right). Furthermore, thanks to Lemma 3.4, if cc is any finite context having α​s\alpha s as an alpha-LIS and if β\beta is any letter, two disjoint cases may occur: either β​c\beta c is a context which has again α​s\alpha s as an alpha-LIS, or β​c\beta c is an external word, cont⁡(β​c)\pref(\beta c) being its own alpha-LIS. This fact contains in germ the announced renewal property of a stable VLMC, as completely formalized in Proposition 3.12, the context alpha-LIS’s constituting renewal patterns of a stable VLMC: once UnU_{n} has begun by a context alpha-LIS, the process will never make use of letters in the past beyond this alpha-LIS.

Remark 3.5.

A general (non-stable) VLMC does not enjoy such a renewal phenomenon.

Consider for instance the context tree built as follows on the alphabet 𝒜={0,1}{\mathscr{A}}=\left\{0,1\right\}. Take the right-infinite word u=0100011011000001⋯u=0100011011000001\cdots obtained by concatenating all finite words ordered by increasing length and alphabetical order: 00, 11, 0000, 0101, 1010, 1111, 000000, etc. Let 𝒯u{\mathscr{T}}_{u} be the context tree spanned by uu – namely the smallest context tree that contains uu as infinite branch. We name 𝒯u{\mathscr{T}}_{u} the filament of all words. Let also UU be a non-null VLMC obtained by probabilising 𝒯u{\mathscr{T}}_{u}. Relatively to this tree, any finite word is the suffix of some internal node. Let thus ww be an arbitrary finite prefix of U0U_{0}, and pp be a finite word such that p​wpw is internal. With positive probability, U|p|=pw⋯U_{|p|}=pw\cdots so that cont⁡(U|p|)\pref\left(U_{|p|}\right) has p​wpw as a strict prefix: the transition from U|p|U_{|p|} to U|p|+1U_{|p|+1} depends on a prefix of U0U_{0} strictly longer than ww. Consequently, no finite prefix of U0U_{0} can play the role of a renewal pattern for the random process UU.

Remark that this situation is generic in the following sense: a right-infinite word rr on {0,1}\left\{0,1\right\} drawn uniformly at random has the following property. For any finite word w∈𝒲w\in{\mathscr{W}}, almost surely, ww is a pattern of rr. Thus, the phenomenon just described for 𝒯u{\mathscr{T}}_{u} holds for any context tree having this infinite word rr as an infinite branch.

Let (Un)n\left(U_{n}\right)_{n} be a stable VLMC. For every nn, let Cn=cont⁡(Un)C_{n}=\pref\left(U_{n}\right). As seen in Proposition 3.1, the process (Cn)n\left(C_{n}\right)_{n} is a Markov chain. In addition, 𝒞f{\mathscr{C}}^{f} is an absorbing set for the chain (Cn)n\left(C_{n}\right)_{n} – as soon as a finite context is seen, all the following contexts will be finite. This is a consequence of the renewal property described above. Therefore, the chain induced by (Cn)n\left(C_{n}\right)_{n} on the absorbing set 𝒞f{\mathscr{C}}^{f} is again a Markov chain that enjoys the following properties.

Lemma 3.6.

Let U=(Un)nU=\left(U_{n}\right)_{n} be a non-null stable VLMC. For any nn, let Cn=cont⁡(Un)C_{n}=\pref\left(U_{n}\right). Then, the Markov chain induced by (Cn)\left(C_{n}\right) on 𝒞f{\mathscr{C}}^{f} is irreducible and aperiodic.

The proof of this lemma is made in Section 4, page 4.2.

In view of this lemma, it would be tempting to try to study the recurrence properties of this Markov chain (Cn)n\left(C_{n}\right)_{n} and then to apply the classical results on countable Markov chains to get a stationary probability measure for the VLMC itself. First, it appears that these recurrence properties are not at all obvious. Moreover, this would mean ignoring the crucial renewal properties of the alpha-LIS process, which are highlighted in Section 3.2.2. That is why it is more fruitful to work with the matrix QQ – in general a smaller matrix than the transition matrix of (Cn)n\left(C_{n}\right)_{n}. Nevertheless, the irreducibility and aperiodicity of (Cn)n\left(C_{n}\right)_{n} will help proving the convergence of the law of (Un)n(U_{n})_{n} towards the invariant measure of the VLMC, in the case of finitely many alpha-LIS (see Theorem 3.24).

Definition 3.7 (stabilizable tree, stabilized of a tree).

A context tree 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} is stabilizable whenever the stable tree ⋃n∈ℕσn​(𝒯)\displaystyle\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\sigma^{n}\left({\mathscr{T}}\right) has at most countably many infinite branches, i.e. when the latter is again a context tree. When this occurs, ⋃n∈ℕσn​(𝒯)\displaystyle\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\sigma^{n}\left({\mathscr{T}}\right) is called the stabilized of 𝒯{\mathscr{T}}; it is the smallest stable context tree containing 𝒯{\mathscr{T}}.

For example, the left-comb is stable. On the contrary, the bamboo blossom is non-stable; it is stabilizable, its stabilized being the double bamboo .

Remark 3.8.

A context tree is not necessarily stabilizable as the following examples, built on the alphabet {0,1}\left\{0,1\right\}, show.

This context tree consists in saturating the infinite word 010212…0k1k⋯010^{2}1^{2}\dots 0^{k}1^{k}\cdots by adding hairs. This filament tree is stabilizable, its stabilized being the context tree having the {0ℓ1k0k+11k+1⋯}\{0^{\ell}1^{k}0^{k+1}1^{k+1}\cdots\} and the {1ℓ0k1k+10k+1⋯}\{1^{\ell}0^{k}1^{k+1}0^{k+1}\cdots\}, k⩾1,0⩽ℓ⩽k−1k\geqslant 1,0\leqslant\ell\leqslant k-1 as internal nodes. Its countably many infinite branches are the 0k​1∞0^{k}1^{\infty} and the 1k​0∞1^{k}0^{\infty}, k⩾0k\geqslant 0.

As defined in Remark 3.5, the filament of all words 𝒯u{\mathscr{T}}_{u} is not stabilizable. Indeed, any finite word belongs to the smallest stable tree that contains 𝒯u{\mathscr{T}}_{u}, the latter being thus the complete tree {0,1}ℕ\left\{0,1\right\}^{\mathbb{N}}, which has uncountably many infinite branches.

Remark 3.9.

Let (𝒯,q)({\mathscr{T}},q) be a stabilizable probabilised context tree and 𝒯^\widehat{{\mathscr{T}}} its stabilized. For every context cc of 𝒯^\widehat{{\mathscr{T}}}, define q^c=qcont⁡(c)\widehat{q}_{c}=q_{\pref(c)} where the function cont is relative to 𝒯{\mathscr{T}}. Then (𝒯,q)({\mathscr{T}},q) and (𝒯^,q^)(\widehat{{\mathscr{T}}},\widehat{q}) define the same VLMC.

This is straightforward because both VLMC, as Markov processes on ℛ{\mathscr{R}}, have the same transition probabilities. The example of the opposite figure illustrates this construction for the bamboo blossom and its stabilized tree, the double bamboo.

3.2 Stable VLMC and Semi-Markov Chains

In this section, semi-Markov chains are defined, following Barbu and Limnios (2008). Section 3.2.2 is devoted to show that any stable VLMC (Un)n⩾0\left(U_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} induces an underlying semi-Markov chain (Zn)n⩾0\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0}: the state space is the set 𝒮{\mathscr{S}} of the context alpha-LIS and ZnZ_{n} is the alpha-LIS of the context cont⁡(Un)\pref\left(U_{n}\right). This semi-Markov chain entirely describes the renewal property that arises in a stable VLMC and gives an explicit interpretation of the matrix QQ. Nevertheless, the trajectories of the VLMC cannot be recovered from those of the induced semi-Markov chain – see Remark 3.13. Despite this, interestingly, when the set of context alpha-LIS is finite, Theorem 3.24 and Theorem 3.29 below make it possible to derive equivalences between NSC for the VLMC to admit a stationary probability measure and NSC for the associated semi-Markov chain to have a limit distribution. This is developed in Section 3.6.

3.2.1 Definitions

Semi-Markov chains are defined thanks to so-called Markov renewal chains – see Barbu and Limnios (2008).

Definition 3.10 (Markov Renewal Chain).

If ℰ{\mathscr{E}} is any set, a Markov chain (Jn,Tn)n⩾0\left(J_{n},T_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} with state space ℰ×ℕ{\mathscr{E}}\times\mathbb{N} is called a (homogeneous) Markov Renewal Chain (shortly MRC) whenever the transition probabilities satisfy: ∀n∈ℕ,∀a,b∈ℰ,∀j,k∈ℕ\forall n\in\mathbb{N},\forall a,b\in{\mathscr{E}},\forall j,k\in\mathbb{N},

𝐏(𝐉𝐧+𝟏=𝐛,𝐓𝐧+𝟏=𝐤|𝐉𝐧=𝐚,𝐓𝐧=𝐣)=𝐏(𝐉𝐧+𝟏=𝐛,𝐓𝐧+𝟏=𝐤|𝐉𝐧=𝐚)=:𝐩𝐚,𝐛(𝐤)\Proba\left(J_{n+1}=b,T_{n+1}=k\big|J_{n}=a,T_{n}=j\right)=\Proba\left(J_{n+1}=b,T_{n+1}=k\big|J_{n}=a\right)=:p_{a,b}(k)

and ∀a,b∈ℰ\forall a,b\in{\mathscr{E}}, pa,b​(0)=0p_{a,b}(0)=0. For such a chain, the family p=(pa,b​(k))a,b∈𝒜,k⩾1p=\left(p_{a,b}(k)\right)_{a,b\in{\mathscr{A}},k\geqslant 1} is called its semi-Markov kernel.

Definition 3.11 (Semi-Markov Chain).

Let (Jn,Tn)n⩾0(J_{n},T_{n})_{n\geqslant 0} be a Markov renewal chain with state space ℰ×ℕ{\mathscr{E}}\times\mathbb{N}. Assume that T0=0T_{0}=0. For any n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, let SnS_{n} be defined by

Sn=∑i=0nTi.S_{n}=\sum_{i=0}^{n}T_{i}.

The semi-Markov chain associated with (Jn,Tn)n⩾0\left(J_{n},T_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} is the ℰ{\mathscr{E}}-valued process (Zj)j⩾0\left(Z_{j}\right)_{j\geqslant 0} defined by

∀j​ such that ​Sn⩽j<Sn+1,Zj=Jn.\forall j\hbox{ such that }S_{n}\leqslant j<S_{n+1},\hskip 14.22636ptZ_{j}=J_{n}.

Note that the sequence (Sn)n⩾0\left(S_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} is almost surely increasing because of the assumption pa,b​(0)=0p_{a,b}(0)=0 (instantaneous transitions are not allowed) that guarantees that Tn⩾1T_{n}\geqslant 1 almost surely, for any n⩾1n\geqslant 1.

The SnS_{n} are jump times, the TnT_{n} are sojourn times in a given state and ZjZ_{j} stagnates at a same state between two successive jump times. The process J=(Jn)nJ=\left(J_{n}\right)_{n}, called the internal (or underlying) chain of the semi-Markov chain (Zn)n\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n}, is a Markov chain on ℰ{\mathscr{E}}. For this Markov chain, the transition probability between states aa and bb is the number pa,b=∑k⩾1pa,b​(k)p_{a,b}=\sum_{k\geqslant 1}p_{a,b}(k).

Definitions 3.10 and 3.11 make transitions of JJ to the same state between time nn and time n+1n+1 possible. Nevertheless, one can boil down to the case where pa,a​(k)=0p_{a,a}(k)=0 for all a∈ℰ,k∈ℕa\in{\mathscr{E}},k\in\mathbb{N}, thus obtaining a semi-Markov chain with true jumps. Indeed, suppose that there exist some a∈ℰa\in{\mathscr{E}} and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that pa,a​(k)≠0p_{a,a}(k)\not=0 for a certain semi-Markov chain (Zn)\left(Z_{n}\right). Consider the chain (Zn′)\left(Z^{\prime}_{n}\right) obtained from (Zn)\left(Z_{n}\right) by forgetting the jumps to the same position. It is the semi-Markov chain associated with the MRC (Jn′,Tn′)n⩾0\left(J^{\prime}_{n},T^{\prime}_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} defined by T0′=0T^{\prime}_{0}=0, J0′=J0J^{\prime}_{0}=J_{0} a.s. and by the following semi-Markov kernel p′p^{\prime}: for a,b∈ℰ,a≠ba,b\in{\mathscr{E}},a\not=b, pa,b′​(1)=pa,b​(1)p^{\prime}_{a,b}(1)=p_{a,b}(1) and for k⩾2k\geqslant 2,

pa,b′​(k)\displaystyle p^{\prime}_{a,b}(k) =𝐏⁡(𝐉𝟏′=𝐛,𝐓𝟏′=𝐤|𝐉𝟎=𝐚)\displaystyle=\Proba\left(J_{1}^{\prime}=b,T^{\prime}_{1}=k\big|J_{0}=a\right) (16)
=pa,b​(k)+∑i=1k−1pa,a​(i)​pa,b′​(k−i)\displaystyle=p_{a,b}(k)+\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}p_{a,a}(i)p^{\prime}_{a,b}(k-i) (17)

(and thus pa,a′​(k)=0p^{\prime}_{a,a}(k)=0 for any k⩾0k\geqslant 0). Note that even if the semi-Markov chains (Zn)\left(Z_{n}\right) and (Zn′)\left(Z^{\prime}_{n}\right) do not have the same internal chains, they get the same trajectories. It is worth noticing that the conditional expectations of T1T_{1} and T1′T_{1}^{\prime} are simultaneously finite or infinite. Indeed, a straightforward calculation from (16) leads to: for a∈ℰa\in{\mathscr{E}},

𝐄⁡(𝐓𝟏′|𝐉𝟎′=𝐚)×(𝟏−∑𝐢⩾𝟏𝐩𝐚,𝐚​(𝐢))=𝐄⁡(𝐓𝟏|𝐉𝟎=𝐚).\Espe\left(T^{\prime}_{1}|J^{\prime}_{0}=a\right)\times\left(1-\sum_{i\geqslant 1}p_{a,a}(i)\right)=\Espe\left(T_{1}|J_{0}=a\right). (18)

Moreover, denoting pa,b=∑k⩾1pa,b​(k)p_{a,b}=\sum_{k\geqslant 1}p_{a,b}(k) and pa,b′=∑k⩾1pa,b′​(k)p^{\prime}_{a,b}=\sum_{k\geqslant 1}p^{\prime}_{a,b}(k), one gets pa,b′=pa,b∑c≠apa,cp^{\prime}_{a,b}=\frac{p_{a,b}}{\sum_{c\not=a}p_{a,c}}, as shortly mentioned in Barbu and Limnios (2008). Since we make use of both versions of a semi-Markov chain in the paper – with true jumps or not, it seemed important to us to devote these few lines to underline how they are connected.

A stable VLMC always induces a semi-Markov chain, as described in the following.

Let (Un)n⩾0\left(U_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} be a stable non-null VLMC and assume that C0=cont⁡(U0)C_{0}=\pref\left(U_{0}\right) is a finite context. with the usual convention that it equals +∞+\infty whenever ∀k>Sn−1,|Ck|>|Ck−1|\forall k>S_{n-1},\left|C_{k}\right|>\left|C_{k-1}\right|. Let also T0=0T_{0}=0 and, for every n⩾1n\geqslant 1, denote by TnT_{n} the difference

3.3 Properties of QQ in the stable case

For a given probabilised context tree, the matrix QQ, that has been defined in Section 2.3 by Formula (9), plays a central role in our main Theorem 2.18. In the case of stable trees, Proposition 3.12 gives a probabilistic interpretation of QQ as the transition matrix of some Markov chain. This section is devoted to gathering properties of QQ (or of the Markov chain QQ is the transition matrix of).

Definition 3.14.

A square (finite or denumerable) matrix (ar,c)r,c\left(a_{r,c}\right)_{r,c} having non-negative entries is said to be row-stochastic whenever all its rows (are summable and) sum to 11, i.e.

∀r,∑car,c=1.\forall r,\penalty\ \sum_{c}a_{r,c}=1.

The following assertion is a consequence of Proposition 3.12, (iii). Remember that the numbers κα​s​(k)\kappa_{\alpha s}(k) are defined by (7). Notice also that one can also make a direct combinatorial proof using Lemma 3.4.

Proposition 3.15.

Let (𝒯,q)\left({\mathscr{T}},q\right) be a stable probabilised context tree. Assume that

∀α​s∈𝒮,limk→∞κα​s​(k)=0.\forall\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}},\penalty\ \penalty\ \lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\kappa_{\alpha s}(k)=0. (24)

Then, the matrix QQ has finite entries and is row-stochastic.

The row-stochasticity of QQ writes

∀α​s∈𝒮,∑β​t∈𝒮Qα​s,β​t=1.\forall\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}},\penalty\ \sum_{\beta t\in{\mathscr{S}}}Q_{\alpha s,\beta t}=1.
Remark 3.16.

Any stochastic matrix with strictly positive coefficients A=(ai,j)i⩾0,j⩾0A=\left(a_{i,j}\right)_{i\geqslant 0,j\geqslant 0} is the matrix QQ associated with some non-null probabilised stable context tree. It may be realised for instance with a left-comb of left-combs as follows.

The left-comb of left-combs is the context tree on the alphabet {0,1}\left\{0,1\right\} as drawn on the left: the finite contexts are the 0p​10q​10^{p}10^{q}1, p,q⩾0p,q\geqslant 0. A left-comb of left-combs is a stable context tree. Its has infinitely many infinite branches, namely 0∞0^{\infty} and the 0p​10∞0^{p}10^{\infty}, p⩾0p\geqslant 0.

For any p,q⩾0p,q\geqslant 0, the alpha-LIS of 0p​10q​10^{p}10^{q}1 is 10q​110^{q}1. In particular, the set 𝒮{\mathscr{S}} of alpha-LIS of contexts is infinite. In this case, for any q⩾0q\geqslant 0, the set of contexts having 10q​110^{q}1 as an alpha-LIS is also infinite.

Probabilise this context tree by a family (qc)c\left(q_{c}\right)_{c} of probability measures on {0,1}\{0,1\}. Denote, for every q,p⩾0q,p\geqslant 0,

cq,p=casc⁡(0p​10q​1)=∏0⩽k⩽p−1q0k​10q​1​(0).c_{q,p}=\casc\left(0^{p}10^{q}1\right)=\prod_{0\leqslant k\leqslant p-1}q_{0^{k}10^{q}1}(0).

Assumption (24) is equivalent to cq,pc_{q,p} converging to 00 when pp tends to ∞\infty, for any qq. The square matrix QQ is infinite and, under the latter assumption, its entries write

Q10q​1,10p​1=casc⁡(10p​10q​1)=cq,p−cq,p+1.Q_{10^{q}1,10^{p}1}=\casc\left(10^{p}10^{q}1\right)=c_{q,p}-c_{q,p+1}.

A row-stochastic positive infinite matrix AA being given, a simple calculation shows that if one defines the probability measures q0p​10q​1q_{0^{p}10^{q}1} of a left-comb of left-combs by

q0p​10q​1​(1)=aq,p1−∑k=0p−1aq,k,q_{0^{p}10^{q}1}(1)=\frac{a_{q,p}}{1-\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}a_{q,k}},

then Q10q​1,10p​1=aq,pQ_{10^{q}1,10^{p}1}=a_{q,p}. The question whether any stochastic matrix (with some zero coefficients) can be realized as the QQ matrix of some non-null stable VLMC seems to be more difficult. Namely, zero coefficients in QQ assuming non-zero qc​(α)q_{c}(\alpha) constraint the shape of the context tree.

Proposition 3.17.

Let (𝒯,q)\left({\mathscr{T}},q\right) be a non-null stable probabilised context tree. Then the matrix QQ is irreducible.

See Section 4 page 4.2 for a proof of this proposition.

3.4 Stationary measure for a stable VLMC vs recurrence of QQ

The following result links the existence and the uniqueness of a stationary probability measure of a VLMC to the recurrence of QQ. Let us recall the definition of recurrence and state a necessary and sufficient condition to get a (unique) invariant probability measure for stable trees. In the sequel, a stochastic matrix is a row-stochastic one – see Definition 3.14. Note that the powers of a stochastic matrix are well defined and also stochastic.

Definition 3.18.

Let A=(ai,j)i,jA=\left(a_{i,j}\right)_{i,j} be a stochastic irreducible countable matrix. Denote by ai,j(k)a_{i,j}^{(k)} the (i,j)(i,j)-th entry of the matrix AkA^{k}. The matrix AA is recurrent whenever there exists ii such that

∑k=1∞ai,i(k)=1.\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}a_{i,i}^{(k)}=1.

Any stochastic irreducible countable matrix may be viewed as the transition matrix of an irreducible Markov chain with countable state space. The recurrence means that there is a state ii (and this is true for every state because of irreducibility) for which the first return time is a.s. finite. When in addition the expectation of the return times are finite, the matrix is classically called positive recurrent.

Theorem 3.19.

Let (𝒯,q)({\mathscr{T}},q) be a non-null probabilised context tree. Assume that 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} is stable. Then, the following assertions are equivalent.

  1. 1.

    The VLMC associated with (𝒯,q)({\mathscr{T}},q) has a unique stationary probability measure

  2. 2.

    The VLMC associated with (𝒯,q)({\mathscr{T}},q) has at least a stationary probability measure

  3. 3.

    The three following conditions are satisfied:

    • (c1)(c_{1})

      the cascade series (6) converge

    • (c2)(c_{2})

      QQ is recurrent

    • (c3)(c_{3})

      ∑α​s∈𝒮vα​s​κα​s<+∞\sum_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}}v_{\alpha s}\kappa_{\alpha s}<+\infty, where (vα​s)α​s\left(v_{\alpha s}\right)_{\alpha s} is the unique non-negative left-fixed vectors of QQ, up to multiplication by a positive real number.

A proof of Theorem 3.19 is given in Section 4.2, page 4.2. Notice that Theorem 3.19 is a direct consequence of Theorem 2.18 and of the fact that QQ is stochastic. In the present article, the stochasticity of QQ is deduced from its interpretation as the transition matrix of some semi-Markov chain (Proposition 3.12). Notice, as already mentioned just before Proposition 3.15, that this stochasticity can also be proved by a direct combinatorial proof. In this sense, Theorem 3.19 can be understood as being independent from the fact that the process (Zn)n\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n} of successive context alpha-LIS of the VLMC (Un)n\left(U_{n}\right)_{n} is a semi-Markov chain (our current notations).

Remark 3.20.

Actually, as shown in the end of the proof, when QQ is recurrent and when the series ∑α​s∈𝒮vα​s​κα​s\sum_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}}v_{\alpha s}\kappa_{\alpha s} converges, then QQ is positive recurrent. Furthermore, all the vα​sv_{\alpha s} are then positive, thanks to Lemma 2.16.

Remark 3.21.

There exist non-null stable probabilised context trees such that (c1)(c_{1}) and (c2)(c_{2}) are fulfilled, but not (c3)(c_{3}), hence with no stationary probability measure. Here is an example based on a left-comb of left-combs, already introduced in Remark 3.16.

Let vp=1p+1−1p+2v_{p}=\frac{1}{p+1}-\frac{1}{p+2} and Rp=∑q⩾pvq=1p+1R_{p}=\sum_{q\geqslant p}v_{q}=\frac{1}{p+1} for every p⩾0p\geqslant 0 (more generally, on can build similar examples based on positive sequences (vp)p\left(v_{p}\right)_{p} such that ∑p⩾0vp=1\sum_{p\geqslant 0}v_{p}=1 and ∑pp​vp\sum_{p}pv_{p} diverges). Define SS by

S⁡(x)=∑q⩾0vq​x1q+1.S(x)=\sum_{q\geqslant 0}v_{q}x^{\frac{1}{q+1}}.

This series is normally convergent on the real interval [0,1][0,1] so that SS is continuous on [0,1][0,1] and satisfies S⁡(0)=0S(0)=0 and S⁡(1)=1S(1)=1. Furthermore, SS is derivable and increasing on [0,1][0,1] since the derived series converges normally on any compact subset of ]0,1]]0,1]. Finally, S⁡(x)⩾vq​x1q+1S(x)\geqslant v_{q}x^{\frac{1}{q+1}} on [0,1][0,1] for every q⩾0q\geqslant 0. Consequently, for every t>0t>0, there exists Ct>0C_{t}>0 such that

∀x∈[0,1],S−1​(x)⩽Ct​xt.\forall x\in[0,1],\penalty\ \penalty\ S^{-1}(x)\leqslant C_{t}x^{t}. (25)

Take now the probabilised left-comb of left-combs defined by the relations (see notations in Remark 3.16)

∀q,p⩾0,cq,p=S−1​(Rp)1q+1.\forall q,p\geqslant 0,\penalty\ c_{q,p}=S^{-1}\left(R_{p}\right)^{\frac{1}{q+1}}.

The definition of SS implies that ∑q⩾0vq​cq,p=Rp\sum_{q\geqslant 0}v_{q}c_{q,p}=R_{p} for every p⩾0p\geqslant 0, which precisely means that v=v​Qv=vQ (the row-vector vv is a left-fixed vector for QQ). Besides, for any q⩾0q\geqslant 0, applying (25) for t=2​(q+1)t=2(q+1) leads to inequalities

∀p⩾0,cq,p⩽C2​(q+1)​(1p+1)2.\forall p\geqslant 0,\penalty\ c_{q,p}\leqslant C_{2(q+1)}\left(\frac{1}{p+1}\right)^{2}.

Thus, the positive sequences (vq)q\left(v_{q}\right)_{q} and (cq,p)p,q\left(c_{q,p}\right)_{p,q} satisfy the following properties.

  1. 1.

    ∀q⩾0,∑pcq,p<∞\forall q\geqslant 0,\sum_{p}c_{q,p}<\infty,

  2. 2.

    ∀p⩾0,∑q⩾0vq​cq,p=∑q⩾pvq\forall p\geqslant 0,\sum_{q\geqslant 0}v_{q}c_{q,p}=\sum_{q\geqslant p}v_{q},

  3. 3.

    ∑qvq<∞\sum_{q}v_{q}<\infty,

In terms of the VLMC, with general notations of Section 2.2, these properties translate into:

  1. 1.

    the cascade series converge (for α​s=10q​1\alpha s=10^{q}1, κα​s=∑pcq,p\kappa_{\alpha s}=\sum_{p}c_{q,p}),

  2. 2.

Therefore, (c1)(c_{1}) is fulfilled and (c3)(c_{3}) is not. Finally, the stability of the context tree and the convergence of cascade series imply the stochasticity of QQ by Proposition 3.15, which force the vector u=(1,1,…,1,…)⊤u=(1,1,\dots,1,\dots)^{\top} to be a right-fixed vector for QQ. Moreover, ⟨v,u⟩=∑α​s∈𝒮vα​s<∞\langle v,u\rangle=\sum_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}}v_{\alpha s}<\infty. Remarking that QQ is aperiodic (for it is strictly positive) and using Remark 7.1.17 p. 207 of Kitchens (1998), this implies the positive recurrence of QQ.

Remark 3.22.

One may wonder whether (c1)⟹(c2)(c_{1})\Longrightarrow(c_{2}). The answer is no. There exists a VLMC defined by a stable tree such that the cascade series converge and the matrix QQ is transient.

To build such an example, recall that, by Remark 3.16, any stochastic matrix with strictly positive coefficients can be realized as the matrix QQ of a stable tree (take for example a left-comb of left-combs). The matrix A=(ai,j)i⩾1,j⩾1A=(a_{i,j})_{i\geqslant 1,j\geqslant 1} defined by

  • •

    ai,i+1=1−1(i+1)2a_{i,i+1}=1-\frac{1}{(i+1)^{2}} for all i⩾1i\geqslant 1,

  • •

    ai,j=1(i+1)2​2j−1a_{i,j}=\frac{1}{(i+1)^{2}2^{j-1}} if j⩾i+2j\geqslant i+2,

  • •

    ai,j=1(i+1)2​2i+1−ja_{i,j}=\frac{1}{(i+1)^{2}2^{i+1-j}} if j⩽ij\leqslant i

is stochastic and transient. Indeed, if one associates a Markov chain to the stochastic matrix AA and if one denotes by T1T_{1} the return time to the first state,

𝐏⁡(𝐓𝟏=∞)⩾∏𝐢⩾𝟏𝐚𝐢,𝐢+𝟏⩾∏𝐢⩾𝟐(𝟏−𝟏𝐢𝟐)=𝟏𝟐.\Proba(T_{1}=\infty)\geqslant\prod_{i\geqslant 1}a_{i,i+1}\geqslant\prod_{i\geqslant 2}\left(1-\frac{1}{i^{2}}\right)=\frac{1}{2}.

Consider now the VLMC defined by a left-comb of left-combs probabilised in the unique way such that Q10q​1,10p​1=aq,pQ_{10^{q}1,10^{p}1}=a_{q,p} for every (p,q)(p,q), like in Remark 3.16. A simple computation shows that the series of cascade converges (geometrically). Simultaneously, since QQ is transient, Theorem 3.19 shows that the VLMC admits no stationary probability measure.

Notice that Theorem 3.19 also provides results for non-stable trees as the following corollary shows, using Remark 3.9.

Corollary 3.23.

Let (𝒯,q)\left({\mathscr{T}},q\right) be a non-null probabilised context tree. Suppose that 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} is stabilizable and denote by 𝒯^\widehat{{\mathscr{T}}} its stabilized. Using the notations of Remark 3.9, if (𝒯^,q^)\left(\widehat{{\mathscr{T}}},\widehat{q}\right) satisfies the conditions of Theorem 3.19, then the VLMC associated with (𝒯,q)\left({\mathscr{T}},q\right) admits a unique invariant probability measure. If not, it does not admit any invariant probability measure. In particular, a VLMC associated to a stabilizable context tree never admits several stationary probability measures.

When the matrix QQ is finite dimensional, stochastic and irreducible, it admits a unique left-fixed vector up to scalar multiplication. This leads to the following theorem.

Theorem 3.24 (finite number of alpha-LIS).

Let (𝒯,q)({\mathscr{T}},q) be a non-null probabilised context tree and U=(Un)nU=\left(U_{n}\right)_{n} be the VLMC it defines. Assume that 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} is stable and that #​𝒮<∞\#{\mathscr{S}}<\infty. Then (i), (ii) and (iii) are equivalent.

(i) UU admits at least a stationary probability measure.

(ii) UU admits a unique stationary probability measure.

(iii) The cascade series (6) converge.

Moreover, whenever one of the previous assertion is true then, for every distribution of U0U_{0} that does not charge any infinite context, for every finite word ww,

𝐏(𝐔𝐧∈𝐰ℛ)⟶𝐧→∞π(𝐰ℛ)\Proba\left(U_{n}\in w{\mathscr{R}}\right)\smash{\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits_{n\to\infty}}\pi\left(w{\mathscr{R}}\right)

where π\pi denotes the unique UU-invariant probability measure.

The proof of Theorem 3.24 is made in Section 4, page 4.2.

Remark 3.25 (Case of finite trees).

Assume that UU is a non-null VLMC defined by a finite context tree. One gets an equivalent process U^\widehat{U} by properly probabilising the stabilized context tree – see Remark 3.9. Since there are finitely many contexts, all the cascade series converge – they are all finite sums. Then, Theorem 3.24 applies, showing that U^\widehat{U} – thus UU – always admits a unique stationary probability measure. This is not surprising because in that case, UU can be seen as an ordinary irreducible Markov chain whose order is the height of its context tree – see Remark 2.4.

The following example shows how one can apply Theorem 3.24.

Example 3.26.

The so-called left-comb of right-combs is particularly simple because if has only one context alpha-LIS. The left-comb of right-combs augmented by a cherry stem, a variation of the former one, gets four context alpha-LIS. Because of Theorem 3.24, both corresponding VLMC have a (unique) stationary probability measure if and only if their cascade series converge.

The left-comb of right-combs, built on the alphabet {0,1}\left\{0,1\right\}, is drawn on the left. Its finite contexts are the 0p​1q​00^{p}1^{q}0, p⩾0p\geqslant 0, q⩾1q\geqslant 1. It has infinitely many infinite branches, namely the 0p​1∞0^{p}1^{\infty}, p⩾0p\geqslant 0. This context tree is stable and all finite contexts have 1010 as an alpha-LIS. The matrix QQ, which is thus 11-dimensional, is reduced to (1)(1). The convergence of the unique cascade series consists in the summability of the double sum

∑p⩾0,q⩾1∏j=0p−1q0j​1q​0​(0)​∏k=1q−1q1k​0​(1).\sum_{p\geqslant 0,q\geqslant 1}\penalty\ \prod_{j=0}^{p-1}q_{0^{j}1^{q}0}(0)\prod_{k=1}^{q-1}q_{1^{k}0}(1).

The left-comb of right-combs with a cherry stem consists in simply replacing the context 1010 of the preceding tree by the cherries 100100 and 101101. The tree is still stable and it has four context alpha-LIS, as resumed in the array.

alpha-LIS α​s\alpha s contexts having α​s\alpha s as an alpha-LIS
100100 100100
101101 101101
010010 0p​100^{p}10, p⩾1p\geqslant 1
110110 0p​1q​00^{p}1^{q}0, p⩾0p\geqslant 0, q⩾2q\geqslant 2

In this last example, the convergence of the cascade series is equivalent to the finiteness of both sums

κ010=∑p⩾1∏k=1p−1q0k​10​(0)andκ110=∑p⩾0,q⩾2∏j=0p−1q0j​1q​0​(0)​∏k=2q−1q1k​0​(1).\kappa_{010}=\sum_{p\geqslant 1}\prod_{k=1}^{p-1}q_{0^{k}10}(0){\rm\penalty\ \penalty\ and\penalty\ \penalty\ }\kappa_{110}=\sum_{p\geqslant 0,\penalty\ q\geqslant 2}\penalty\ \prod_{j=0}^{p-1}q_{0^{j}1^{q}0}(0)\prod_{k=2}^{q-1}q_{1^{k}0}(1).

3.5 A semi-Markov chain is a stable VLMC

In this section, it is shown that any semi-Markov chain on a finite state space is a VLMC associated with some particular infinite stable probabilised context tree. Consequently, one deduces from Theorem 3.24 a necessary and sufficient condition for a non-null semi-Markov chain to admit a limit distribution. This condition already appears in Barbu and Limnios (2008).

Definition 3.27.

If b⩾2b\geqslant 2, the bb-comb is the context tree on an alphabet 𝒜{\mathscr{A}} of cardinality bb having {αkβ:α,β∈𝒜,α≠β,k⩾1}\left\{\alpha^{k}\beta:\alpha,\beta\in{\mathscr{A}},\alpha\neq\beta,\penalty\ k\geqslant 1\right\} as a set of finite contexts.

Theorem 3.28.

Let bb be an integer, b⩾2b\geqslant 2. Every semi-Markov chain with true jumps on a state space having bb elements is the process of initial letters of a VLMC on the bb-comb.

In the proof, placed in Section 4 on page 4.2, the correspondance between the bb-comb and the semi-Markov chain is made explicit. More precisely, the probability distributions at each context of the bb-comb are given, such that the initial letter process of the VLMC has the same distribution as a given semi-Markov chain with bb states.

Theorem 3.29.

Let (Zn)n⩾0\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} be a semi-Markov chain with true jumps on a finite state space ℰ{\mathscr{E}}. Denote by p=(pα,β​(k))α,β∈ℰ,k⩾1p=\left(p_{\alpha,\beta}(k)\right)_{\alpha,\beta\in{\mathscr{E}},k\geqslant 1} its semi-Markov kernel and assume that for any α,β∈ℰ,α≠β,k⩾1\alpha,\beta\in{\mathscr{E}},\alpha\not=\beta,k\geqslant 1, pα,β​(k)≠0p_{\alpha,\beta}(k)\not=0. Then, the following properties are equivalent.

  • (i)

    (Zn)n⩾0\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} admits a limit distribution.

  • (ii)

    For every α∈ℰ\alpha\in{\mathscr{E}}, the series

    mα:=∑k⩾1k⁡(∑γ∈ℰpα,γ​(k))m_{\alpha}:=\sum_{k\geqslant 1}k\left(\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathscr{E}}}p_{\alpha,\gamma}(k)\right)

    is convergent.

A proof of Theorem 3.29 can be found in Section 4, page 4.2.

Remark 3.30.

The sum mαm_{\alpha} is readily seen as a mean sojourn time: mα=𝐄⁡(𝐓𝟏|𝐉𝟎=α)m_{\alpha}=\Espe\left(T_{1}\big|J_{0}=\alpha\right). Theorem 3.29 establishes that mα<∞m_{\alpha}<\infty for any α∈ℰ\alpha\in{\mathscr{E}} is a necessary and sufficient condition for a semi-Markov chain with true jumps and with a positive semi-Markov kernel to admit a limit distribution. Thus, the sufficient assumption mα<∞m_{\alpha}<\infty for any α∈ℰ\alpha\in{\mathscr{E}} in Barbu and Limnios (2008) becomes a NSC when also assuming that for any α,β∈ℰ,α≠β,k⩾1\alpha,\beta\in{\mathscr{E}},\alpha\not=\beta,k\geqslant 1, pα,β​(k)≠0p_{\alpha,\beta}(k)\not=0.

3.6 From a VLMC to its induced SMC and back (finite number of alpha-LIS)

The above allows us to go a little further for a non-null stable VLMC (Un)(U_{n}) and its associated semi-Markov chain (Zn)(Z_{n}) of its successive context alpha-LIS, in the case when there are finitely many alpha-LIS’s. Remark 3.13 asserts that one cannot recover the VLMC (Un)\left(U_{n}\right) from the semi-Markov chain (Zn)\left(Z_{n}\right) (see Section 3.2.2). Nevertheless, one may ask whether the NSC for existence of a limit distribution for the semi-Markov chain (Zn)\left(Z_{n}\right) is the same as the NSC for existence and unicity of a stationary probability measure for the VLMC (Un)\left(U_{n}\right). The answer is yes.

Indeed, under the assumptions of Theorem 3.24 (finite number of alpha-LIS), the induced 𝒮{\mathscr{S}}-valued semi-Markov chain (Zn)\left(Z_{n}\right) has a finite number of states. Thus, Theorem 3.29 applies and gives a NSC for (Zn′)\left(Z^{\prime}_{n}\right), the semi-Markov chain with true jumps deduced from (Zn)\left(Z_{n}\right) by formulas (16). This NSC writes mα​s′<+∞m^{\prime}_{\alpha s}<+\infty where

mα​s′=𝐄⁡(𝐓𝟏′|𝐉𝟎′=α​𝐬)=∑𝐤⩾𝟏𝐤⁡(∑β​𝐭≠α​𝐬𝐩α​𝐬,β​𝐭′).m^{\prime}_{\alpha s}=\Espe\left(T_{1}^{\prime}|J_{0}^{\prime}=\alpha s\right)=\sum_{k\geqslant 1}k\left(\sum_{\beta t\not=\alpha s}p^{\prime}_{\alpha s,\beta t}\right).

Besides, thanks to (18), mα​s′<+∞m^{\prime}_{\alpha s}<+\infty is equivalent to mα​s<+∞m_{\alpha s}<+\infty since, as already noticed in Remark 3.30, mα​s=𝐄⁡(𝐓𝟏|𝐉𝟎=α​𝐬)m_{\alpha s}=\Espe\left(T_{1}|J_{0}=\alpha s\right). Thanks to Proposition 3.12(i) and its proof, 𝐄⁡(𝐓𝟏|𝐉𝟎=α​𝐬)=κα​𝐬\Espe\left(T_{1}|J_{0}=\alpha s\right)=\kappa_{\alpha s}, so that

κα​s=mα​s.\kappa_{\alpha s}=m_{\alpha s}.

Moreover, in Theorem 3.24, κα​s<+∞\kappa_{\alpha s}<+\infty for any α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}} is the NSC for existence and unicity of a stationary probability measure for a stable VLMC with a finite number of alpha-LIS. Summarizing, the following holds.

Proposition 3.31.

Let (Un)n\left(U_{n}\right)_{n} be a non-null stable VLMC admitting a finite number of alpha-LIS. Let (Zn)n\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n} be the 𝒮{\mathscr{S}}-valued process of its alpha-LIS – see Formula (19). Then, the following properties are equivalent.

  • (i)

    (Un)n⩾0\left(U_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} admits a unique stationary probability measure.

  • (ii)

    The cascade series (6) converge.

  • (iii)

    (Zn)n⩾0\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} admits a limit distribution.

4.2 Proofs of Section 3 (stable case)

Proof of Proposition 3.1.

(i)⟹(i​i)(i)\implies(ii). Take c∈𝒞c\in{\mathscr{C}} and α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}}. Assume that α​c∈ℐ\alpha c\in{\mathscr{I}}. (i​i)⟹(i)(ii)\implies(i). Take α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}} and w∈𝒲w\in{\mathscr{W}} such that α​w∈𝒯\alpha w\in{\mathscr{T}}.
