It comes α​c​w′∈𝒯\alpha cw^{\prime}\in{\mathscr{T}}, which implies α​c∈ℐ\alpha c\in{\mathscr{I}} and this contradicts (i​i)(ii).

(i)⇔(i​i​i)(i)\iff(iii) is straightforward.

(i​i)⟹(i​v)(ii)\implies(iv) What needs to be proved is that cont⁡(Un+1)\pref\left(U_{n+1}\right) only depends on UnU_{n} through cont⁡(Un)\pref\left(U_{n}\right). In other words, we shall prove that for all s∈ℛ,α∈𝒜s\in{\mathscr{R}},\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}}, cont⁡(α​s)\pref\left(\alpha s\right) only depends on ss through cont⁡(s)\pref(s). This is clear because

cont⁡(α​s)=cont⁡(α​cont⁡(s)).\pref(\alpha s)=\pref\left(\alpha\pref(s)\right).

Indeed, cont⁡(s)∈𝒞\pref(s)\in{\mathscr{C}} and if cont⁡(s)∈𝒞f\pref(s)\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f}, then (ii) implies α​cont⁡(s)∉ℐ\alpha\pref(s)\notin{\mathscr{I}} (if cont⁡(s)\pref(s) is an infinite context, this means that s=cont⁡(s)s=\pref(s) and the above equality is straightforward). Therefore α​cont⁡(s)\alpha\pref(s) writes c​wcw with c∈𝒞c\in{\mathscr{C}} and w∈𝒲w\in{\mathscr{W}}. On one hand, this entails cont⁡(α​cont⁡(s))=c\pref\left(\alpha\pref(s)\right)=c. On the other hand, this means that c​wcw is a prefix of α​s\alpha s thus cont⁡(α​s)=c\pref(\alpha s)=c.

(i​v)⟹(i​i)(iv)\implies(ii) We shall prove the contrapositive. Assume there exists c∈𝒞fc\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f} and α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}} such that α​c∈ℐ\alpha c\in{\mathscr{I}}. Let s∈ℛs\in{\mathscr{R}} such that cont⁡(s)=c\pref(s)=c. As α​c∈ℐ\alpha c\in{\mathscr{I}}, cont⁡(α​s)\pref(\alpha s) is a context which has α​c\alpha c as a strict prefix. Therefore, cont⁡(α​s)\pref(\alpha s) does not only depend on cont⁡(s)\pref(s), but on a prefix of ss strictly longer than cont⁡(s)\pref(s). Thus, conditionally to CnC_{n}, the transition to the context Cn+1C_{n+1} does not depend on CnC_{n} but on a strictly longer prefix of UnU_{n}. This proves that (Cn)n\left(C_{n}\right)_{n} is not Markovian. ∎

Proof of Lemma 3.4.

1. Assume that tt is a context LIS such that c=t⋯c=t\cdots, then, by definition of a context LIS, there exists α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}} such that α​t\alpha t is a context alpha-LIS. Since 𝒯{\mathscr{T}} is stable, Lemma 3.3 implies that α​t\alpha t is a context, therefore α​c∉𝒞\alpha c\notin{\mathscr{C}} because two different contexts cannot be prefix of one another. Thus 𝒜c≠∅{\mathscr{A}}_{c}\neq\emptyset.

Aperiodicity. Let us prove that, given c∈𝒞fc\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f}, the g.c.d. of the lengths of the admissible paths from cc to itself equals 11. Let kk be the length of cc. Proof of Proposition 3.17.

Let UU be the VLMC defined by (𝒯,q)\left({\mathscr{T}},q\right). As before in the text, for every nn, let Cn=cont⁡(Un)C_{n}=\pref\left(U_{n}\right) and ZnZ_{n} be the alpha-LIS of CnC_{n}. Let also JJ be the internal chain of the semi-Markov process Z=(Zn)nZ=\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n} – see Definition 3.11 and Proposition 3.12. Since the context tree is assumed to be stable, any context alpha-LIS is a finite context (Lemma 3.3). Besides, the Markov chain C=(Cn)nC=\left(C_{n}\right)_{n} induced on 𝒞f{\mathscr{C}}^{f} has been shown to be irreducible (Proposition 3.6). Therefore, two arbitrary finite contexts are joined by an admissible path relative to the Markov chain CC. In particular, two arbitrary context alpha-LIS α​s\alpha s and β​t\beta t are joined by an admissible path relative to the Markov chain CC. Taking the alpha-LIS of such a path of contexts provide a path of context alpha-LIS joining α​s\alpha s to β​t\beta t for the process ZZ, which means that conditioning by Z0=α​sZ_{0}=\alpha s, there is some n⩾0n\geqslant 0 such that the event Zn=β​tZ_{n}=\beta t occurs with positive probability. Restricting this path to jump times provides an admissible path joining α​s\alpha s to β​t\beta t relative to the Markov process JJ. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.19 (Invariant probability measures for a stable VLMC).

(3.⟹\implies1.) Since QQ is recurrent and irreducible, there exists a unique line ℝ​v\mathbb{R}v of left-fixed vectors for QQ. Let v=(vα​s)α​s∈𝒮v=\left(v_{\alpha s}\right)_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}} be such a vector having non-negative entries (see for example (Seneta, 2006, Theorem 5.4)). Theorem 2.18(ii) coupled with the assumption on the series ∑α​s∈𝒮vα​s​κα​s\sum_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}}v_{\alpha s}\kappa_{\alpha s} entails directly the existence and uniqueness of a stationary probability measure.

(2.⟹\implies3.) If there exists a stationary probability measure, then Theorem 2.18(i) and Lemma 2.16 assert that the cascade series converge and that QQ admits at least one left-fixed vector vv with positive entries such that ∑α​s∈𝒮vα​s​κα​s<∞\sum_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}}v_{\alpha s}\kappa_{\alpha s}<\infty. Besides, every κα​s\kappa_{\alpha s} is greater than 11. Indeed, the cascade of any alpha-LIS is 11 and, in the stable case, any alpha-LIS is a context (Lemma 3.3). Thus, vv is summable and QQ is positive recurrent (see for instance (Seneta, 2006, Corollary of Theorem 5.5)). Since it is irreducible (Proposition 3.17), it admits a unique direction of left-fixed vectors ℝ​v\mathbb{R}v, proving (3.) by Theorem 2.18. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.28 (A semi-Markov chain on a finite state space is a stable VLMC).

Let (Zn)n⩾0\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} be a semi-Markov chain with true jumps on a state space of cardinality bb. Without lack of generality, for technical convenience, take 𝒜=ℤ/b​ℤ{\mathscr{A}}=\mathbb{Z}/b\mathbb{Z}. Denote by (JN)N⩾0\left(J_{N}\right)_{N\geqslant 0} the internal chain of (Zn)n\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n}, namely the process of the successive different states of (Zn)n⩾0\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} and by (TN)N⩾0\left(T_{N}\right)_{N\geqslant 0} the process of the successive sojourn times in the visited states, with the convention T0=0T_{0}=0. Assuming that (Zn)n⩾0\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} is semi-Markov amounts to supposing that almost surely, for every N⩾0N\geqslant 0, α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}}, k⩾1k\geqslant 1,

𝐏(𝐉𝐍+𝟏=α,𝐓𝐍+𝟏=𝐤|𝐉𝟎,⋯,𝐉𝐍,𝐓𝟏,⋯,𝐓𝐍)=𝐏(𝐉𝐍+𝟏=α,𝐓𝐍+𝟏=𝐤|𝐉𝐍).\Proba\left(J_{N+1}=\alpha,T_{N+1}=k\big|J_{0},\cdots,J_{N},T_{1},\cdots,T_{N}\right)=\Proba\left(J_{N+1}=\alpha,T_{N+1}=k\big|J_{N}\right).

Denote by p=(pα,β​(k))α,β∈𝒜,k⩾1p=\left(p_{\alpha,\beta}(k)\right)_{\alpha,\beta\in{\mathscr{A}},k\geqslant 1} the semi-Markov kernel of the process:

pα,β​(k)=𝐏⁡(𝐉𝐍+𝟏=β,𝐓𝐍+𝟏=𝐤|𝐉𝐍=α).p_{\alpha,\beta}(k)=\Proba\left(J_{N+1}=\beta,T_{N+1}=k\big|J_{N}=\alpha\right).

For any n⩾0n\geqslant 0, define the right-infinite random sequence

Vn=ZnZn−1⋯Z1Z0(1+Z0)Y−2,V_{n}=Z_{n}Z_{n-1}\cdots Z_{1}Z_{0}\left(1+Z_{0}\right)Y_{-2},

where Y−2Y_{-2} is any non atomic distribution on ℛ{\mathscr{R}}. Remember that the process (Zn)n⩾0\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} takes its values in the set 𝒜=ℤ/b​ℤ{\mathscr{A}}=\mathbb{Z}/b\mathbb{Z}. The semi-Markov property of (Zn)n⩾0\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} guarantees that the ℛ{\mathscr{R}}-valued process (Vn)n⩾0\left(V_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} is Markovian.

Define now (Un)n⩾0\left(U_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} as the VLMC on the bb-comb with alphabet 𝒜{\mathscr{A}}, with the following parameters. As an initial state, take U0=Z0​(1+Z0)​Y−2U_{0}=Z_{0}\left(1+Z_{0}\right)Y_{-2}. As a transition probability associated with the context βℓ​γ\beta^{\ell}\gamma where β,γ∈𝒜\beta,\gamma\in{\mathscr{A}}, β≠γ\beta\neq\gamma and ℓ⩾1\ell\geqslant 1, take the probability measure qβℓ​γq_{\beta^{\ell}\gamma} on 𝒜{\mathscr{A}}:

∀α∈𝒜,qβℓ​γ​(α)={pβ,α​(ℓ)∑k⩾ℓ(∑δ∈𝒜pβ,δ​(k))​if​α≠β1−∑δ∈𝒜pβ,δ​(ℓ)∑k⩾ℓ(∑δ∈𝒜pβ,δ​(k))=∑k⩾ℓ+1(∑δ∈𝒜pβ,δ​(k))∑k⩾ℓ(∑δ∈𝒜pβ,δ​(k))​if​α=β.\forall\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}},q_{\beta^{\ell}\gamma}(\alpha)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\displaystyle\frac{p_{\beta,\alpha}(\ell)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k\geqslant\ell}\left(\sum_{\delta\in{\mathscr{A}}}p_{\beta,\delta}(k)\right)}{\rm\penalty\ if\penalty\ }\alpha\neq\beta\\[50.0pt] \displaystyle 1-\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{\delta\in{\mathscr{A}}}p_{\beta,\delta}(\ell)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k\geqslant\ell}\left(\sum_{\delta\in{\mathscr{A}}}p_{\beta,\delta}(k)\right)}=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{k\geqslant\ell+1}\left(\sum_{\delta\in{\mathscr{A}}}p_{\beta,\delta}(k)\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k\geqslant\ell}\left(\sum_{\delta\in{\mathscr{A}}}p_{\beta,\delta}(k)\right)}{\rm\penalty\ if\penalty\ }\alpha=\beta.\end{array}\right. (38)

Note that qβℓ​γq_{\beta^{\ell}\gamma} does not depend on γ\gamma and that the convergence of the series is guaranteed by the properties of the semi-Markov kernel pp.

We show that both ℛ{\mathscr{R}}-valued Markov processes (Un)n⩾0\left(U_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} and (Vn)n⩾0\left(V_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} have the same distribution stating that, for any α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}} and n⩾0n\geqslant 0, almost surely,

𝐏⁡(𝐕𝐧+𝟏=α​𝐕𝐧|𝐕𝐧)=𝐪cont⁡(𝐕𝐧)​(α).\Proba\left(V_{n+1}=\alpha V_{n}\big|V_{n}\right)=q_{\pref\left(V_{n}\right)}(\alpha).

Since V0V_{0} and U0U_{0} have the same distribution, this will entail the result.

Let r∈ℛr\in{\mathscr{R}}, not of the form β∞\beta^{\infty}, β∈𝒜\beta\in{\mathscr{A}}; write r=βℓ​sr=\beta^{\ell}s where ℓ⩾1\ell\geqslant 1, β∈𝒜\beta\in{\mathscr{A}} and s∈ℛs\in{\mathscr{R}} starts with a letter different from β\beta. Denote, by SnS_{n} the partial sum of TkT_{k}, as in Definition 3.11. For any α∈𝒜\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}}, α≠β\alpha\neq\beta and for any n⩾0n\geqslant 0, as soon as NN is such that SN⩽n⩽SN+1−1S_{N}\leqslant n\leqslant S_{N+1}-1,

𝐏(𝐕𝐧+𝟏=α𝐕𝐧|𝐕𝐧=𝐫)=𝐏(𝐉𝐍+𝟏=α,𝐓𝐍+𝟏=ℓ|𝐉𝐍=β,𝐓𝐍+𝟏⩾ℓ,𝐕𝐧−ℓ=𝐬).\Proba\left(V_{n+1}=\alpha V_{n}\big|V_{n}=r\right)=\Proba\left(J_{N+1}=\alpha,T_{N+1}=\ell\big|J_{N}=\beta,T_{N+1}\geqslant\ell,V_{n-\ell}=s\right).

Because of the semi-Markov property, this entails that

𝐏(𝐕𝐧+𝟏=α𝐕𝐧|𝐕𝐧=𝐫)=𝐏(𝐉𝐍+𝟏=α,𝐓𝐍+𝟏=ℓ|𝐉𝐍=β,𝐓𝐍+𝟏⩾ℓ).\Proba\left(V_{n+1}=\alpha V_{n}\big|V_{n}=r\right)=\Proba\left(J_{N+1}=\alpha,T_{N+1}=\ell\big|J_{N}=\beta,T_{N+1}\geqslant\ell\right).

Using the semi-Markov kernel, this leads to

𝐏⁡(𝐕𝐧+𝟏=α​𝐕𝐧|𝐕𝐧=𝐫)=𝐏⁡(𝐉𝐍+𝟏=α,𝐓𝐍+𝟏=ℓ|𝐉𝐍=β)𝐏⁡(𝐓𝐍+𝟏⩾ℓ|𝐉𝐍=β)=𝐩β,α​(ℓ)∑δ∈𝒜∑𝐤⩾ℓ𝐩β,δ​(𝐤).\Proba\left(V_{n+1}=\alpha V_{n}\big|V_{n}=r\right)=\frac{\Proba\left(J_{N+1}=\alpha,T_{N+1}=\ell\big|J_{N}=\beta\right)}{\Proba\left(T_{N+1}\geqslant\ell\big|J_{N}=\beta\right)}=\frac{p_{\beta,\alpha}(\ell)}{\displaystyle\sum_{\delta\in{\mathscr{A}}}\sum_{k\geqslant\ell}p_{\beta,\delta}(k)}.

This shows that Formulae (38) are the suitable ones to ensure that both Markov processes (Un)n⩾0\left(U_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} and (Vn)n⩾0\left(V_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} have the same distribution. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.29 (Limit distribution of a semi-Markov chain).

Let bb be the cardinal of the state space ℰ{\mathscr{E}}. Let UU be the VLMC defined on the bb-comb (Definition 3.27) by the transition probabilities of Formula (38). This context tree (the bb-comb) is defined on the alphabet 𝒜=ℰ{\mathscr{A}}={\mathscr{E}}; it admits a finite number of context alpha-LIS, namely the words α​β\alpha\beta where α\alpha and β\beta are two distincts elements of ℰ{\mathscr{E}}; furthermore, in this tree, the set of contexts having α​β\alpha\beta as an alpha-LIS is {αℓ​β:ℓ⩾1}\left\{\alpha^{\ell}\beta:\penalty\ \ell\geqslant 1\right\}. The processes (Zn)n\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n} and UU are related by Theorem 3.28. Moreover, Theorem 3.24 applies to UU. Indeed, thanks to Formulas (38), the assumption on the positivity of the semi-Markov kernel pp implies that the associated VLMC UU is non-null.

By Theorem 3.24, the convergence of the cascade series implies the convergence 𝐏⁡(𝐔𝐧∈𝐰​ℛ)→π⁡(𝐰​ℛ)\Proba\left(U_{n}\in w{\mathscr{R}}\right)\to\pi\left(w{\mathscr{R}}\right) when nn tends to infinity, for any finite word ww. As a consequence, as soon as the cascade series converge, 𝐏⁡(𝐙𝐧=β|𝐙𝟎=α)\Proba\left(Z_{n}=\beta|Z_{0}=\alpha\right) converges to π⁡(β​ℛ)\pi\left(\beta{\mathscr{R}}\right) when nn tends to infinity, and this limit does not depend on α\alpha. In other words, (Zn)n⩾0\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n\geqslant 0} admits (π⁡(β​ℛ))β∈ℰ\left(\pi\left(\beta{\mathscr{R}}\right)\right)_{\beta\in{\mathscr{E}}} as a limit distribution.

Conversely, assume that (Zn)n\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n} admits a limit distribution μ\mu. In terms of the VLMC (Un)n\left(U_{n}\right)_{n}, this implies that 𝐏⁡(𝐔𝐧∈α​ℛ)\Proba\left(U_{n}\in\alpha{\mathscr{R}}\right) tends to μ⁡(α)\mu(\alpha) when nn tends to infinity, for every α∈ℰ\alpha\in{\mathscr{E}}. Let α,β∈ℰ\alpha,\beta\in{\mathscr{E}} be two distinct letters, so that α​β∈𝒮\alpha\beta\in{\mathscr{S}}. For every n⩾1n\geqslant 1,

𝐏⁡(𝐔𝐧∈α​β​ℛ)=𝐏⁡(𝐙𝐧=α,𝐙𝐧−𝟏=β)=𝐩β,α​(𝟏)​𝐏⁡(𝐙𝐧−𝟏=β)\Proba\left(U_{n}\in\alpha\beta{\mathscr{R}}\right)=\Proba\left(Z_{n}=\alpha,Z_{n-1}=\beta\right)=p_{\beta,\alpha}(1)\Proba\left(Z_{n-1}=\beta\right)

so that

𝐏(𝐔𝐧∈αβℛ)⟶𝐧→∞𝐩β,α(𝟏)μ(β).\Proba\left(U_{n}\in\alpha\beta{\mathscr{R}}\right)\smash{\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits_{n\to\infty}}p_{\beta,\alpha}(1)\mu(\beta). (39)

This has two consequences.

Firstly, μ⁡(α)≠0\mu(\alpha)\neq 0 for every α∈ℰ\alpha\in{\mathscr{E}}. Indeed, since μ\mu is a probability measure, all these numbers cannot simultaneously vanish; let thus β∈ℰ\beta\in{\mathscr{E}} such that μ⁡(β)≠0\mu(\beta)\neq 0. Let also α∈ℰ∖{β}\alpha\in{\mathscr{E}}\setminus\left\{\beta\right\}. For any n⩾1n\geqslant 1, as before,

𝐏⁡(𝐙𝐧​𝐙𝐧−𝟏=α​β)=𝐩β,α​(𝟏)​𝐏⁡(𝐙𝐧−𝟏=β).\Proba\left(Z_{n}Z_{n-1}=\alpha\beta\right)=p_{\beta,\alpha}(1)\Proba\left(Z_{n-1}=\beta\right).

Assume that μ⁡(α)=0\mu(\alpha)=0. Since 𝐏⁡(𝐙𝐧​𝐙𝐧−𝟏=α​β)⩽𝐏⁡(𝐙𝐧=α)\Proba\left(Z_{n}Z_{n-1}=\alpha\beta\right)\leqslant\Proba\left(Z_{n}=\alpha\right), the left hand side of this equality tends to 00 when nn tends to infinity, which is impossible because the limit right hand side, namely pβ,α​(1)​μ​(β)p_{\beta,\alpha}(1)\mu(\beta), is non-null. Thus, μ⁡(α)≠0\mu(\alpha)\neq 0.

Secondly, for every ℓ⩾1\ell\geqslant 1,

𝐏(𝐔𝐧∈αℓβℛ)=casc(αℓβ)𝐏(𝐔𝐧−𝐥+𝟏∈αβℛ)⟶𝐧→∞casc(αℓβ)𝐩β,α(𝟏)μ(β).\Proba\left(U_{n}\in\alpha^{\ell}\beta{\mathscr{R}}\right)=\casc\left(\alpha^{\ell}\beta\right)\Proba\left(U_{n-l+1}\in\alpha\beta{\mathscr{R}}\right)\smash{\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits_{n\to\infty}}\casc\left(\alpha^{\ell}\beta\right)p_{\beta,\alpha}(1)\mu(\beta).

Thus, if LL is a positive integer,

∑ℓ=1L𝐏(𝐔𝐧∈αℓβℛ)⟶𝐧→∞[∑ℓ=𝟏𝐋casc(αℓβ)]𝐩β,α(𝟏)μ(β).\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\Proba\left(U_{n}\in\alpha^{\ell}\beta{\mathscr{R}}\right)\smash{\mathop{\longrightarrow}\limits_{n\to\infty}}\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\casc\left(\alpha^{\ell}\beta\right)\right]p_{\beta,\alpha}(1)\mu(\beta). (40)

For any nn, the left hand side of Formula (40) if less than 11 because it is bounded above by the whole sum ∑c∈𝒞f𝐏⁡(𝐔𝐧∈𝐜​ℛ)+∑𝐜∈𝒞𝐢𝐏⁡(𝐔𝐧=𝐜)\sum_{c\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f}}\Proba\left(U_{n}\in c{\mathscr{R}}\right)+\sum_{c\in{\mathscr{C}}^{i}}\Proba\left(U_{n}=c\right) which equals 11 by disjoint union. Thus, the right hand side is also bounded. In particular, since pβ,α​(1)p_{\beta,\alpha}(1) and μ⁡(β)\mu(\beta) are non-null, the series of positive numbers ∑ℓcasc⁡(αℓ​β)\sum_{\ell}\casc\left(\alpha^{\ell}\beta\right) converge. Besides, the cascade series of the context alpha-LIS α​β\alpha\beta is precisely κα​β=∑ℓ⩾1casc⁡(αℓ​β)\kappa_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{\ell\geqslant 1}\casc\left(\alpha^{\ell}\beta\right). This allows us to conclude that the existence of a limit distribution for the process (Zn)n\left(Z_{n}\right)_{n} implies the convergence of all the cascade series.

It suffices now to show that condition (i​i)(ii) is equivalent to the convergence of every cascade series

∑ℓ⩾1casc⁡(αℓ​β).\sum_{\ell\geqslant 1}\casc\left(\alpha^{\ell}\beta\right).

Let α\alpha and β\beta be two distinct elements of 𝒜{\mathscr{A}}. For any ℓ⩾1\ell\geqslant 1, since

casc⁡(αℓ​β)=∏k=1ℓ−1qαk​β​(α),\casc\left(\alpha^{\ell}\beta\right)=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell-1}q_{\alpha^{k}\beta}(\alpha),

an immediate reading of Formula (38) shows that

casc⁡(αℓ​β)=∑k⩾ℓ(∑γ∈𝒜pα,γ​(k))∑k⩾1(∑γ∈𝒜pα,γ​(k)),\casc\left(\alpha^{\ell}\beta\right)=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{k\geqslant\ell}\left(\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathscr{A}}}p_{\alpha,\gamma}(k)\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k\geqslant 1}\left(\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathscr{A}}}p_{\alpha,\gamma}(k)\right)},

so that the sum of these cascades writes

∑ℓ⩾1casc⁡(αℓ​β)=∑k⩾1k⁡(∑γ∈𝒜pα,γ​(k))∑k⩾1(∑γ∈𝒜pα,γ​(k))∈[0,+∞],\sum_{\ell\geqslant 1}\casc\left(\alpha^{\ell}\beta\right)=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{k\geqslant 1}k\left(\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathscr{A}}}p_{\alpha,\gamma}(k)\right)}{\displaystyle\sum_{k\geqslant 1}\left(\sum_{\gamma\in{\mathscr{A}}}p_{\alpha,\gamma}(k)\right)}\in[0,+\infty],

leading to the result. Note that the cascade series ∑ℓ⩾1casc⁡(αℓ​β)\sum_{\ell\geqslant 1}\casc\left(\alpha^{\ell}\beta\right) does not depend on β\beta, because all the probability measures one has to associate with the leaves of a given context of the comb are all the same ones, as can be seen on Formula (38). ∎

5 Open problems and conjectures

5.1 Right-fixed vectors for QQ

Take a probabilised context tree. When the tree is stable and whenever the sequence (κα​s​(n))n\left(\kappa_{\alpha s}(n)\right)_{n} converge to 00 for every α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}, the square matrix QQ can be seen as the transition matrix of some 𝒮{\mathscr{S}}-valued Markov chain, so that it turns out to be stochastic – see Proposition 3.15. This is not true in general if one removes the stability assumption (Remark 2.19). We nevertheless make the following conjecture.

Conjecture 5.1.

For any probabilised context tree, whenever the sequence (κα​s​(n))n\left(\kappa_{\alpha s}(n)\right)_{n} converge to 00 for every α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}, the matrix QQ always admits 11 as a right-eigenvalue.

In particular, thanks to Theorem 2.18, if a context tree has a finite set of alpha-LIS and if this conjecture is true, then the corresponding VLMC always admits at least one invariant probability measure as soon as its (finitely many) cascade series converge.

5.2 Convergence of cascade series

Consider two very simple examples on the alphabet 𝒜={0,1}{\mathscr{A}}=\left\{0,1\right\}, pictured hereunder: the left comb and the bamboo blossom – see Cénac et al. (2012) for a complete treatment of stationary probability measures for these VLMC. It turns out that the left comb gets one context alpha-LIS and thus one cascade series, that can be convergent or not depending on the distributions qcq_{c}. The bamboo blossom gets two context alpha-LIS, both cascade series being always convergent with geometrical rates whatever the (non-null) distributions qcq_{c} are. This phenomenon, which seems to be generalizable, leads us to the following conjecture.

Conjecture 5.2.

Take a non-null probabilised context tree. When the tree does not have any infinite shift-stable subtree, all the cascade series converge, with geometrical rates.

5.3 Vanishing of cascades and σ\sigma-finite invariant measures

Take a stable probabilised context tree. As recalled just above (Section 5.1), whenever the sequence (κα​s​(n))n\left(\kappa_{\alpha s}(n)\right)_{n} converge to 00 for every α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}} (we call this assumption vanishing of cascades), the square matrix QQ is stochastic by Proposition 3.15. Moreover, Theorem 2.18 or Theorem 3.19 asserts that the convergence of cascade series is a necessary condition for the VLMC to admit an invariant probability measure. As stated herunder, the vanishing of cascades is conjectured to be a necessary condition for the VLMC to admit an invariant σ\sigma-finite measure.

Conjecture 5.3.

Let UU be a VLMC defined by a probabilised stable context tree. Assume that UU admits an invariant σ\sigma-finite measure. Then, for every α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}, the sequence (κα​s​(n))n\left(\kappa_{\alpha s}(n)\right)_{n} tends to 00 when nn tends to infinity (and, consequently, QQ is stochastic).

6 Appendix: an example of invariant σ\sigma-finite measure that charges irrational infinite contexts

A soon as a non-null VLMC admits an invariant probability measure, all infinite words are negligible – see Lemma 2.16(ii). Besides, the same argument as in the proof of that lemma shows that an invariant σ\sigma-finite measure always vanishes on rational right-infinite words, i.e. on eventually periodic words. This appendix provides an example of non-null VLMC that admits an invariant σ\sigma-finite measure which gets positive values on infinitely many (necessarily irrational) contexts44 4 In particular, one cannot get rid of the finiteness assumption of an invariant measure to prove Lemma 2.16(ii)..

In this appendix, a “σ\sigma-finite measure” denotes a positive non-zero measure on ℛ{\mathscr{R}} which is finite on all cylinders c​ℛc{\mathscr{R}} based on finite contexts cc, and also, necessarily, on infinite contexts. In particular, since the contexts induce a partition of ℛ{\mathscr{R}}, such a measure is truly σ\sigma-finite. As usual in the field of Markov chains, when UU is a VLMC, the definition of an UU-invariant probability measure can be extended to σ\sigma-finite measures using the transition probability kernel PUP_{U}, defined by

PU(r,B)=∑α∈𝒜qcont⁡(r)(α)11{αr∈B}P_{U}(r,B)=\sum_{\alpha\in{\mathscr{A}}}q_{\pref(r)}(\alpha)\hbox{\rm\small 1\kern-3.23753pt\normalsize 1}_{\{\alpha r\in B\}}

on Borel sets BB and right-infinite words rr: this kernel acts on σ\sigma-finite measures π\pi through the formula

π​PU​(B):=∫ℛPU​(x,B)​𝑑π​(x)\pi P_{U}(B):=\int_{{\mathscr{R}}}P_{U}(x,B)d\pi(x)

(this is an action on the right), and a σ\sigma-finite measure π\pi is said UU-invariant whenever π​PU=π\pi P_{U}=\pi.

In what follows, we describe the announced example in the form of a sequence of hints and assertions that can be easily (but sometimes laboriously) verified.

Consider the irrational right-infinite word a=10102​103​104​…a=1010^{2}10^{3}10^{4}\dots. Define as follows the stabilised arithmetic tree, denoted by 𝒯a{\mathscr{T}}_{a}: it is the stable context tree on the alphabet 𝒜={0,1}{\mathscr{A}}=\left\{0,1\right\} spanned by aa, i.e. the smallest context tree that contains all the shifted words σn​(a)\sigma^{n}(a), n⩾0n\geqslant 0 (see Definition 2.6). On the left side of the following picture, one can find drawings of the successive context trees tnt_{n} spanned by the shifted infinite word σn​(a)\sigma^{n}(a), n⩾1n\geqslant 1. They are used to give a representation of 𝒯a{\mathscr{T}}_{a} on the right side of the picture.

Computing the contexts leads to show that 𝒯a{\mathscr{T}}_{a} admits two one-parameter families of context alpha-LIS, namely 0q​10q​10^{q}10^{q}1, q⩾0q\geqslant 0 and 10N​10N+210^{N}10^{N+2}, N⩾1N\geqslant 1. They are coloured red in the pictures. Thus the related matrix QQ is infinite – see (9) for a definition of QQ. Moreover, the infinite contexts of 𝒯a{\mathscr{T}}_{a} are the following ones: on one side, the 0∞0^{\infty} and the 0n​10∞0^{n}10^{\infty}, n⩾0n\geqslant 0 which are rational; on the other side, the σn​(a)\sigma^{n}(a) which are irrational.

Given a non-null probabilising of 𝒯a{\mathscr{T}}_{a}, assume that an invariant σ\sigma-finite measure μ\mu exists. Reasoning like in the proof of Theorem 2.18, for every α​s∈𝒮\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}, decompose the number μ⁡(α​s​ℛ)\mu\left(\alpha s{\mathscr{R}}\right) through the partition of s​ℛs{\mathscr{R}} induced by cylinders based on finite contexts that have ss as a prefix and by such infinite contexts as well. These writings show that QQ’s entries are necessarily finite (sums of summable families) as well as the sums ∑c∈𝒞i,c=s​…qc​(α)​μ​(c)\sum_{c\in{\mathscr{C}}^{i},\penalty\ c=s\dots}q_{c}(\alpha)\mu(c). Note further that QQ is row-stochastic because 𝒯a{\mathscr{T}}_{a} is a stable tree (see Proposition 3.15). Since all infinite contexts are shifted from aa and since μ\mu is invariant, all the numbers μ⁡(c)\mu(c), c∈𝒞ic\in{\mathscr{C}}^{i} can be written as μ⁡(c)=μ⁡(a)pc\mu(c)=\frac{\mu(a)}{p_{c}} where pcp_{c} is a finite product of qσk​(a)​(β)q_{\sigma^{k}(a)}(\beta), k⩾0k\geqslant 0, β∈𝒜\beta\in{\mathscr{A}}. Consequently, all the sums

ℓα​s:=∑c∈𝒞ic=s​…qc​(α)pc\ell_{\alpha s}:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{c\in{\mathscr{C}}^{i}}\\[1.0pt] {c=s\dots}\end{subarray}}\frac{q_{c}(\alpha)}{p_{c}}

are also finite – note that the sums ℓ0q​10q​1\ell_{0^{q}10^{q}1}, q⩾1q\geqslant 1 are reduced to a single term, all other ℓα​s\ell_{\alpha s}’s being true infinite sums.

Finally, like in the proof of Theorem 2.18, the above decompositions lead to the following statement: a σ\sigma-finite measure μ\mu is invariant if and only if it satisfies the (infinite) matricial equation

μ⁡(a)​ℓ+μ𝒮​Q=μ𝒮\mu(a)\ell+\mu_{{\mathscr{S}}}Q=\mu_{{\mathscr{S}}} (41)

where ℓ\ell and μ𝒮\mu_{{\mathscr{S}}} denote the infinite row-vectors ℓ=(ℓα​s)α​s∈𝒮\ell=\left(\ell_{\alpha s}\right)_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}} and μ𝒮=(μ⁡(α​s​ℛ))α​s∈𝒮\mu_{{\mathscr{S}}}=\left(\mu\left(\alpha s{\mathscr{R}}\right)\right)_{\alpha s\in{\mathscr{S}}}. Notice that after a straightforward continuation of the function ff to σ\sigma-finite measures, μ𝒮=f⁡(μ)\mu_{{\mathscr{S}}}=f(\mu) (see (13)). Using the vocabulary of Kitchens (1998), one finally gets the following result.

Proposition 6.1.

Let UU be some non-null VLMC defined from the context tree 𝒯a{\mathscr{T}}_{a} and let QQ be its QQ-matrix (see (9)).

(i) If QQ is positive recurrent, then UU admits a unique half-line of invariant σ\sigma-finite measures. All of them are finite ones.

(ii) If QQ is null recurrent, then UU admits a unique half-line of invariant σ\sigma-finite measures. None of them are finite ones, but they turn all infinite words negligeable.

(iii) If QQ is transient, then UU does not admit any invariant probability measure.

We build an example of VLMC on 𝒯a{\mathscr{T}}_{a} that admits an invariant σ\sigma-finite measure that charges (all) irrational infinite contexts. Proposition 6.1 shows that the corresponding QQ-matrix is necessarily transient.

To exhibit such an example, one first have to compute the “form” of QQ (check which entries vanish, see below) and to make explicit the way how ℓ\ell’s and QQ’s entries are expressed in terms of the qcq_{c}. This being done, one sees that any row-stochastic matrix AA having the form of QQ (same positive entries, same zero ones) is the QQ-matrix of a probabilised context tree 𝒯a{\mathscr{T}}_{a} (choice of the qcq_{c}, c∈𝒞fc\in{\mathscr{C}}^{f}). Furthermore, if XX is any positive row-vector that satisfies X​A<XXA<X (strict inequality for every coordinate), the vector X−X​AX-XA can be chosen as the ℓ\ell-vector of such a probabilised 𝒯a{\mathscr{T}}_{a} (choice of the qcq_{c}, c∈𝒞ic\in{\mathscr{C}}^{i}).

Therefore, thanks to Equation (41), an example of invariant σ\sigma-finite measure that charges (all) irrational infinite contexts is given by any row-stochastic matrix AA having the required form, together with a positive row-vector XX that satisfies X​A<XXA<X. Note that such an AA is necessarily transient and that a corresponding XX has necessarily non summable coordinates (see Kitchens (1998)). Below, we give such a matrix AA.
